dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo finally looked up, the spare grip still in his fingers, and let his expression arrange itself into something approximating offense.

"Slow," he repeated. "You say that like it was a character flaw." He set the grip down on the bench and leaned back on his heels, arms folding across his chest. "I was *deliberate*. There is a difference, Reyes, and it is the difference between fencing and flailing."

He gestured vaguely toward the empty piste behind them, where the strip lights hummed their low fluorescent buzz.

"You had the attack. I chose to make you work for it. That's not slowness, that's... patience." He said the word like it had a chalky residue on it. "It's what separates a good second fencer from a mediocre one."

He stood, brushing dust off his trousers, and fell into step beside Reyes instead of ahead. That was unusual. Corvo usually took the lead on the walk to the car, as if proximity to the exit were a competitive advantage.

"So," he said. "Three-two. I still want that third touch adjudicated."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, nudging his shoulder with mine as we walk. "Patience, sure. Looked a lot like hesitation from my angle." I glance over at him, a smirk playing on my lips. "And I'm not driving you to the adjudication committee, so drop it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a breath through his nose, half-laugh, half-protest, and did not nudge back. He noted this. He noted it the way he noted everything about Reyes, with the quiet precision of a man who had spent years studying the way an opponent held a blade before the lights went on.

"From your angle," he conceded, still walking. "Fair. You were closer."

The parking lot was cold and the car headlights were already dying, one by one, around them. Somewhere inside, the cleaning crew had left the lights low and the mirrors dark.

He stopped beside Reyes' car, though not to drive it. He just stopped, hands in his pockets, and looked at Reyes with that particular expression he reserved for things he was choosing not to fight about.

"Here's what I'll say," Corvo started, then stopped himself, repositioning. "I'll say that the third touch was *contested*, and that is a different word than 'generous.' The committee would want that nuance."

He waited. The silence between them was not the comfortable kind. It had a texture, like the fine grit of a scuffed piste surface.

"Though," he added, quieter, and he shifted his weight from one foot to the other in a way that was decidedly unlike Corvo, "you did have a good bout. The riposte in the second exchange was clean. Textbook."

He almost looked pleased saying it. Almost.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let his hands stay in his pockets, even though the grip was gone, even though his fingers were suddenly purposeless and he did not know what to do with that.

"Slow," he tried again, and this time the word came out flat, stripped of its usual defensive bounce. "You keep returning to that word like it's a weapon. Like if you say it enough, it becomes a touch on the scorecard."

He looked down at the empty grip lying on the asphalt between them, then back at Reyes. The parking lot lights did not reach the far corner where they stood, so the shadows were deep and the distance between them was small and very definite.

"You want to know what I actually saw on the piste?" he said. "I saw you telegraphing the riposte in the second exchange. Half a beat. You got lucky I didn't see it, or I did see it and chose to let it pass because it was close." He paused, jaw working slightly. "So don't tell me about my slowness when your own blade was doing the talking."

He stepped closer. Not much. Enough that Reyes could smell the iron of the sweat under his jacket, the cold air of the lot, the faint old smell of leather and grip tape that lived permanently in his hair.

"Slow all evening," Corvo repeated, and this time there was something under it that was not irritation. "Maybe. Maybe that's what it was." He tilted his head, studying Reyes the way he studied a line of attack. "Or maybe I was just waiting to see if you'd say something other than 'three-two.'"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, closing the rest of the distance between us. "I saw you telegraphing your patience," I say, my voice low. "Half a beat."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's jaw set, and for a moment the two of them stood in the dark like fencers waiting for the halt command.

"Half a beat," he echoed. "You've been stealing my vocabulary all evening. Patience. Half a beat. You fence like a man quoting a textbook back at you."

But he did not step away. That was the thing, and Corvo felt it the way he felt a pressure point before the blade arrived, a warning his body registered before his mind caught up.

He reached out and caught the front of Reyes' jacket, not gripping hard, just enough to anchor the proximity between them. His thumb brushed the collar, a nervous motion disguised as casualness.

"You want to know the truth?" he said, and his voice had dropped into the register he used when the piste was empty and only the two of them remained. "I wasn't slow. I was *thinking*. Every single exchange, I was calculating whether you'd go for the counter or the retreat, and I wanted to know which one you'd choose before I committed."

He released the jacket. Looked away. The cold air moved between them.

"Which is exactly the same thing as being slow," he added, "but I'm telling you that now because I'm tired of pretending it was something more dignified."

He exhaled, long and slow, fogging briefly in the air.

"Your riposte was good," he said again, and this time there was no *almost* in his voice. "And I let it land because I wanted to see what you'd do with a clean touch. And you did the right thing. You stopped."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo hit the bench first, his back against the cold metal, and immediately looked as though the position was one he had planned. It was not. He was a man who stood in doorways and paced strips, never a man who sat.

He pulled the mask from his head and let it dangle by its strap, not putting it down, just holding it the way one held a foil between parries.

"I said you stopped," he muttered, staring at the fluorescent tubes above them. "That was the point. That was the whole point of letting that riposte land."

He swung his legs out, boots scuffing the floor, and turned his head to look at Reyes. The changing room was small, lit harshly, and the distance between them was the length of a bench.

"You could have kept going," Corvo said. "After the second touch, you had the line open. Anyone else would have pushed. Anyone else, you'd have scored a three-one." He made a small gesture with the mask, a dismissive flick. "But you stopped. You called it even and let me have the third on merit."

He said *on merit* like it tasted wrong, like he was chewing on it to see if it was real.

"So don't sit there acting like I was generous," he continued, and there was heat in it now, but different heat than the piste had produced. "I was generous once, tonight. And it was right here, in front of you, and you took it without asking."

He set the mask down beside his own bag, deliberately, precisely, aligning the strap with the seam of the vinyl.

"Three-two," he said, quietly. "And I want it on record that I didn't hate you tonight. I want that on record somewhere, because by morning I'll want it to have never happened."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I reach over and snatch the mask from his hands, tossing it toward our bags with a clatter. "I stopped because I was waiting for you to say something first."

I lean in, elbows on my knees, and look at him directly. "You're not the only one who can be patient."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound that might have been a laugh or might have been him trying to breathe normally after holding it for several minutes.

"Waiting," he repeated. "You were *waiting*. For me. To say something." He shook his head slowly, staring at the bench between them. "Reyes, I have been saying something to you for four years. It's just usually in the language of lunges and ripostes and the word 'generous' used generously about your footwork."

He picked at a thread on his trousers. A nervous habit he did not have. Another data point he was not going to examine too closely.

"You wanted me to say what?" he asked, and the question came out rougher than intended. He cleared his throat and tried again, lower. "Because I can tell you right now, in plain words, that the last time I let you have a clean exchange it was not because I was slow or generous or patient. It was because watching you fence is the only thing all week that makes me forget I'm second best in a sport that doesn't care about feelings."

He looked up then, fully, and the fluorescent light caught the scar along his eyebrow, the one from a misjudged parry in '19 that Reyes knew about because Reyes had been on the strip when it happened.

"And you," Corvo continued, "you've spent four years making me feel like a second-best instructor in front of my students. Do you know what that does to a man? It makes him want to either throw you through a wall or, apparently," he gestured vaguely at the space between them, "sit on a bench with you at ten at night and say things he's never said to another living person."

He leaned forward, elbows on his own knees now, mirroring Reyes without meaning to.

"So yes," he said. "Something first. You wanted something first." His voice dropped to almost nothing. "I was trying to figure out what it was, and you kept calling it three-two."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hand shot up to catch the bench edge, his knuckles whitening against the metal.

"That's," he started, and the word came out strangled, half-formed, nothing like the measured vocabulary he deployed on the piste. "That's not an exchange. That's not a touch. That's not anything that goes on a scorecard."

He swallowed hard. His mask sat abandoned by Reyes' bag, and the thought that it had come between them in that way, had been the object of their snatching and tossing, was absurd and made him want to laugh again.

He caught Reyes' wrist instead. Not to stop them. His fingers closed around the bone gently, a fencer's grip, precise and controlled, even now.

"You're doing it on purpose," he said, and there was a wrecked quality to his voice, stripped of its usual authority. "You've been doing it all night. Stealing my words, stealing my blade, stealing my patience. And now you're doing this because I finally said something plain and you want me to say it again with my hands."

His breath was coming uneven. The changing room smelled of disinfectant and old rubber and the metallic tang of two people who had been working hard for three hours.

He leaned into Reyes' mouth instead of pulling away, and it was clumsy, and it tasted of the energy drink Reyes had likely been nursing all evening, and Corvo would have hated admitting that it was fine.

"Slow," he breathed against Reyes' lips. "Finally slow. For once, actually slow."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to speak, my hand still tangled in his jacket. "And you're still talking when you could be doing."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's mouth opened and closed once, a useless sound, and he pressed his forehead against Reyes' shoulder instead of answering.

"Doing," he repeated, and the word came out wrecked, stripped of any authority whatsoever. "You want me to stop fencing with words and start fencing with, what. My hands? In a changing room?"

He made a noise like a man being slowly suffocated by his own competence.

"Fine," he said, and his grip on Reyes' wrist tightened, then released, then tightened again in a pattern that had nothing to do with technique and everything to do with nerves. "Fine. I'll do."

He rolled his weight and pulled Reyes down with him, one arm hooking around the back of Reyes' neck to hold them in place while the other fumbled against Reyes' jacket, searching for the clasp with the dexterity of a man who had spent four years gripping a blade and zero years gripping anything else.

"You know what the worst part is," Corvo managed, voice muffled against Reyes' collarbone. "I'm going to be terrible at this. I've never, this isn't something you practice in a salle. There's no bout sheet. No scoring lights."

His fingers found what they were looking for.

"I'm a second fencer," he said, and there was a broken laugh in it. "I'm the one who waits and calculates and makes sure I have the right answer before I commit. And right now I am committing to absolutely nothing I've prepared for."

But he did not pull back. He did not retreat to the defensive posture he had held all evening, all night, all four years. He rolled Reyes under him properly, on the cold bench, with the metal groaning slightly, and looked down with eyes that were very wide and very bright and very unlike the cold calculating ones that had read the piste so accurately.

"Three-two," he whispered. "Last time I'm using that score tonight."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went rigid under Reyes' hands, the bench creaking again, and for one full heartbeat the only sound was the fluorescent hum and two people breathing too loudly.

"Concede," he said flatly, staring at the ceiling. "I concede. I concede right here, right now, in front of the mirror that's going to show my coach the rest of the week."

But his hips shifted, not retreating, adjusting, finding the new angle Reyes had forced on him. His jaw worked. His shoulders, which had been tense and defensive all evening, loosened into the metal with a sound like a weapon laid down.

"Prove the point properly," he echoed, and there was a dangerous note in it now, not anger, the other thing. The thing Reyes had been teasing all night without naming it. "You want me to stop calculating and just, commit?"

He arched, pressing into the restraint, feeling Reyes' strength across his chest. His wrists were pinned, but his body was not.

"Then don't stop," Corvo said, and his voice was low and rough and entirely stripped of its fencing-instructor register. "Because I'm going to stop being the one who waits. I'm going to stop being the one who says the word 'generous' and means it as a complaint."

He moved against the pins, not fighting them, working with them, using the bench to roll them both into a new position where Reyes was beneath him, where his wrists were free, where he could finally reach for Reyes' collar with both hands and hold on like the whole evening had been building toward exactly this.

"Four years," he said, forehead dropping to meet Reyes'. "Four years of three-two and adjudication committees and you making me look like a man who needs his ripostes explained." His thumb pressed flat against Reyes' throat, not squeezing, just marking the spot, just claiming it. "And I have spent four years saying 'you were slow' and meaning 'you made me feel alive' and you never once caught the actual words."

He kissed Reyes, hard, with the flat of his mouth and the full weight of his body and no calculation whatsoever.

"Three-two was wrong," he said against Reyes' lips. "It was two-two. It's been two-two since '19. Since the scar." He pulled back far enough to look at Reyes, really look, with the wide bright eyes of a man who had finally thrown away his blade and was standing in the open. "I wanted you to see me fence properly. Not in front of students. Not with a score to manage. Just, this. You and me and a bench that groans."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get a hand in his hair and pull, not enough to hurt, just enough to make him look at me. "Then stop scoring points and do something about it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo obeyed the pull of Reyes' fingers and looked up, really looked up, into the fluorescent glare and the small cramped space of the changing room.

"About it," he repeated, as though tasting the words. His chest was heaving under Reyes' hand. His jaw was unguarded in a way it had not been all night, all evening, all four years of measured ripostes and deliberate exchanges.

He shifted his weight and settled fully over Reyes, knees bracketing, hands on either side of Reyes' face now, thumbs resting on the cheekbones like a man steadying himself before a final attack.

"About it," he said again, quieter. "Yes. About it."

He kissed Reyes once more, slower this time, deliberate in the way Corvo used to be deliberate on the piste, but without the calculation, without the waiting-for-the-opponent-to-move. Just forward motion. Just commitment.

When he broke away, he was breathless and his eyes were wet in a way he would deny later if asked.

"I'm going to be very bad at this," he said, and there was a laugh in it, wrecked and genuine. "I've rehearsed fencing with you for four years and I have no practice whatsoever for this. For you, like, here, without masks, without rules, without someone to call a halt."

He pressed his forehead to Reyes' forehead, their breaths mingling in the cold air.

"So tell me what to do," Corvo said. "Actually tell me. Because for once, I will follow instructions instead of pretending I already knew the answer."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo closed his eyes and nodded against Reyes' forehead like he had received a valid command.

"Don't stop," he repeated, and then he meant it, and stopped being the man who calculated and committed fully instead, pulling Reyes' jacket open with both hands and working fast, fumbling with the clasp he had fumbled with before but with purpose now, with a kind of desperate efficiency.

"God, this is embarrassing," he muttered, but he was already moving, already stripping down with the same relentless forward motion he brought to every bout. "I'm an instructor. I stand in front of teenagers in a full uniform. And I am undressing in a changing room with the lights on like a man who has never done this in his life."

He sat back on his heels, fully exposed, and let the jacket fall. His ribs were narrow and lean, built for the long reaches of epee, and the scar along his eyebrow was visible now in the harsh light, and the smaller scar on his left forearm where a blade had slipped in a bout he refused to discuss with anyone.

"You were never slow," Reyes had said. And Corvo had never believed it until this bench, this room, this pair of hands in his hair.

He reached for Reyes, pulling them up into him, wrapping his legs around Reyes' waist and his arms around Reyes' neck, and made no attempt to be graceful.

"Tell me if I'm doing it wrong," he said, teeth against Reyes' jaw, voice wrecked. "I will take criticism. I will take it the way I take it on the piste, which is badly and loudly."

He kissed Reyes' throat, then lower, and his mouth was clumsy and he knew it was clumsy and he did not care, because for the first time in four years the exchange was even and neither of them was keeping score.

Reyes' hands moved against his back, and Corvo arched into them, a full-body answer, no riposte, no parry, no deliberate half-beat. Just open. Just exposed. Just Reyes.

"Two-two," he gasped, and then laughed into the skin of Reyes' shoulder. "I'm going to say that so often you'll hate me."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I bite his shoulder, right over the scar I know is there. "You talk more when you're losing," I say, my voice rough. "Always have."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo yelped, a sound of genuine protest, and his fingers dug into Reyes' back hard enough to bruise.

"Over the scar," he hissed. "You bit the scar. That's not, that's like attacking a disarmed fencer. That's unsportsmanlike."

He was laughing, though. He was laughing and gasping and his face was flushed under the fluorescent light and he looked nothing like the composed instructor who had rewrapped a grip an hour ago out of pure habit.

"Always talk when I'm losing," he repeated, and his voice cracked on the words, and he pulled Reyes closer, tangled them together properly this time, legs and arms and breaths all one unit. "Maybe I'm not losing. Maybe I'm just, narrating the bout."

He kissed Reyes' collarbone, then the hollow beneath it, moving down with the steady pressure of a man who had finally stopped waiting for the opponent to telegraph.

"You want me to be quiet?" Corvo asked, and he was not quiet, he never would be, he was a man who needed to say the words even while his body did the work. "Because I can be quiet. I can be the one who doesn't talk. I can be the second fencer one more time."

But even as he said it, he was already moving against Reyes, already making his own attack, already committing to the line without calculation.

"Two-two," he said again, breathless, forehead pressed to Reyes' shoulder. "I'm conceding. I concede everything. You've won. You've been winning since '19 and I was too proud to call it."

His hands found Reyes' hips, pulling them flush against his own, and he let out a sound that was not a word, not a score, not a fencing term of any kind.

"Say it again," Corvo whispered. "Say I'm not losing. Say it so I have to believe it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I grab his jaw and make him look at me. "You're not losing. You're finally where you should've been four years ago."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's eyes held Reyes' for a long moment, the fluorescent light catching the wetness in them, the scar along his eyebrow, the unguarded expression of a man who had been told the truth and was choosing whether to believe it.

"Where I should've been," he repeated, and his voice was barely above a whisper now, stripped of every defensive layer he had worn all evening.

He let go of Reyes' hips and slid his hands up to cup Reyes' face, thumbs smoothing the cheekbones, fingers threading into the hair at the nape. It was the tenderest thing he had ever done in the salle. He would remember that later, in the shower, in the car, in the mornings where he would wake and have to decide whether the night had been real or whether Reyes had dreamed it.

"I should've been here," Corvo said. "In '19. When you got that touch on the left shoulder and I didn't call the halt. I should've been here instead of standing at the side of the piste pretending I was analyzing your footwork."

He kissed Reyes, slow and deep and with no plan, and his body answered the kiss the way it had answered Reyes all night, with clumsy commitment and zero technique.

"I was terrified," he admitted between kisses, forehead resting against Reyes' temple. "Four years of coming here and watching you fence and thinking that if I ever said it out loud, I'd lose the one thing I had left. The rivalry. The argument. The only reason I went to the salle on Tuesday nights instead of home."

He pulled back far enough to look at Reyes properly.

"So," Corvo said, and he made a small sound, almost a laugh, almost a sob. "Three-two. Adjudication committee. You were slow. You were fast. You were generous. I was patient."

His hands tightened in Reyes' hair, gentle but firm.

"I'm not doing that anymore. Whatever this is, it's not a bout. There's no score to keep and no one to call a halt and no fourth touch to argue about."

He leaned down and kissed Reyes again, and this time he did not pull away, did not narrate, did not calculate. He just held on and gave himself without reservation, and the bench groaned, and the fluorescent lights hummed, and the door remained unlocked for anyone who might walk in on two rival instructors having lost their arguments, their scores, and their four-year war all at once.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let him hold on until he finally runs out of words. Then I push him onto his back on the bench and look him over. "See? Better than a scorecard."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: He stepped closer. Not much. Enough that Reyes could smell the iron of the sweat under his jacket

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: He set the mask down beside his own bag, deliberately, precisely, aligning the strap with the seam of the vinyl.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: He leaned into Reyes' mouth instead of pulling away

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Four years of three-two and adjudication committees

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: He kissed Reyes' throat, then lower, and his mouth was clumsy

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at the phone in his hand, then at Bee, then at the floor of the hallway where the lightbulb had been dead since February. He didn't step aside.

"Last time you did, you wanted to borrow my drill. You wanted it at eight in the morning on a Sunday." He held up a finger. "I was sleeping. That was allowed."

"That was three years ago, when I was allowed to be on this list."

"Of course you were." He said it flatly, which was worse than if he'd been angry. "You were on the list until you weren't. That's not my fault for not texting you back about a drill."

Ilya finally moved, but only to lean against the doorframe, crossing his arms. The flat behind him smelled of coffee and the faint chemical ghost of the cleaning products he'd bought to replace the ones Bee had always used, which he'd noticed and resented with equal clarity.

"So." He nodded toward the hallway. "Are you going to tell me why you're here, or do we need to go through the whole catalogue first? Because I have things to get to."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I'm here because you owe me money, Ilya." I cross my own arms, matching his posture. "Don't pretend you forgot. The deposit for that gig *you* flaked on."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya uncrossed his arms slowly, as though the motion cost him something. He pressed the back of his hand against his forehead, then dropped it.

"I didn't flake," he said. "The venue fell through. You were there, you remember, you were in the van with me."

"The venue fell through and you didn't tell me for six hours. Six hours, Ilya. I had booked a taxi, I'd eaten lunch I could have saved, and I was sitting in a car park in Islington wondering if you'd had an accident."

"I was at the venue. Trying to get it back together." He stepped fully into the doorway now, no longer leaning, no longer blocking. "And I did get it back together, for most of the band. For us, the two of us, it was gone. We both knew that."

He looked past Bee, into the hallway, at the dead lightbulb, at the neighbour's door that would have buzzed if it had worked.

"Okay," he said. "You're right. I owe you."

The admission hung in the air with the particular weight of something he had clearly been rehearsing against himself.

"Forty pounds," he said. "Plus whatever the taxi was."

"Sixty."

"Fine." He reached into his jacket pocket and produced his phone, not to text, but to open his banking app. "You can Venmo it. Or I can transfer."

He watched Bee's face the whole time he did it, measuring the reaction, waiting for the thing he was bracing for, which was not gratitude and not anger but the small, tired disappointment that this was what they were doing now. Trading money like it was the last honest thing between them.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went rigid, one hand still holding his phone with the banking app open on the screen. He didn't pull away. He didn't kiss back, exactly, but he didn't push Bee away either, and his mouth was warm against hers with the faint residue of the coffee he'd been drinking.

When they broke apart, he exhaled through his nose and stared at a point just above Bee's shoulder.

"Don't do that," he said quietly.

"I'm not doing anything. I kissed you."

"That's what you're doing. That's exactly what you're doing." He set his phone down on the shoebox by the door, the deposit for his own life, and stepped back into his flat, closing the door partway behind him so that the corridor light stayed on them both. "You were angry, you got your money, and now you're kissing me because you wanted something from me and I gave it to you, and the transaction feels incomplete."

"It felt like a good continuation of the argument."

Ilya laughed, a short, ugly sound. "You're so good at that. You're so good at making it sound like I'm the one being unreasonable for wanting boundaries."

"Was I unreasonable?"

"You kissed me in a corridor after asking me for money I owed you. In a building with a broken buzzer so that anyone in the flats above us could have come downstairs to investigate the noise." He shook his head. "We broke up eleven months ago, Bee. Eleven months. You didn't call, you didn't text, and now you've turned up wanting forty pounds and a kiss like it's Tuesday."

"Seventy pounds and a kiss," Bee corrected, though the words came out softer than intended.

Ilya looked at him. Really looked, for a long second, and there was something in his expression that wasn't anger, which was somehow more unsettling than anger would have been.

"Seventy pounds and a kiss," he repeated, as though tasting it. "Okay." He pushed the door open wider, stepping aside. "Come in. But we're not sleeping over, and we're not pretending this is what we used to be."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step past him into the flat, my shoulder brushing his chest. "I wasn't planning on pretending."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let Bee pass with his hand hovering near the small of Bee's back, not touching, not quite. He led the way into the kitchen, which was smaller than the memory of it, or perhaps Bee had simply been closer to him before.

"Sit," he said, gesturing at the table where a half-eaten sandwich and a laptop sat side by side. "I'll make tea. Do you want the good mugs or the ones from the charity shop?"

"Whatever's closest."

"The good ones. Obviously." Ilya opened the cupboard, and there they were, the matching set with the little blue flowers that Bee had bought them from a market in Camden, three years and change ago. He set one on the counter without commenting on it.

Bee sat at the table. The laptop screen was still active, some spreadsheet Ilya had been working on, and there was a coffee mug next to it with the ring of foam that meant it had been abandoned mid-sip. Everything in the flat was in its place, in a way that felt like evidence rather than tidiness.

"You kept the mug," Bee said.

Ilya poured boiling water without looking up. "I kept most things. I didn't go through and throw them out like we were cleaning a flat before listing it." He set the cup in front of Bee. The tea was green, the kind Bee had always claimed to hate but drank anyway. "There's honey in the drawer."

Bee pushed the honey jar across the table with two fingers. "I remember."

"You remember a lot of things." Ilya pulled out the chair opposite and sat down, elbows on the table now, head in his hands. "You remember the drill. You remember the taxi. You remember I owe you seventy pounds." He let out a breath. "I remember you stopped answering my texts in month four. I remember I sent eleven of them and you sent back one, two words, *not now*, and I understood that to mean forever."

Bee wrapped both hands around the mug. "I didn't understand what I meant until you were gone."

"That's not fair to say to my face."

"I know. It's fair to say, though."

Ilya looked up. He was trying to be stern, and failing, the way a person fails when the sternness is only a container for something else entirely.

"So you're here," he said. "For the money, which you have, and for a kiss, which you've had, and for the tea, which you're drinking. What else are you here for? Because I want to know before you start making it complicated again."

Bee took a sip. "I'm here because I missed you and I didn't know how to say that without making it sound like a demand."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya caught Bee's wrists against the doorframe, not to stop him, but to feel where Bee's pulse was running.

"Slow down," he said, though his own breathing was uneven. "We're in a hallway. The neighbours can hear everything."

"They can hear the broken buzzer buzz too. Which never happens."

Ilya pressed his forehead to Bee's shoulder blade, the skin there warm and bare, and closed his eyes. His hands slid from Bee's wrists down to his elbows, holding on, steadying.

"You're not going to say anything?" he asked. "You're not going to pull away or tell me this is a bad idea or remind me about the argument we were having forty seconds ago?"

"Is it a bad idea?"

Ilya didn't answer. He pulled Bee against him properly then, fully, the door swinging shut behind them with a soft click, and kissed the side of Bee's neck with a mouth that tasted of green tea and honey.

"It's a very bad idea," he said against Bee's skin. "I'm not going to stop you."

He backed them against the wall of the hallway, one hand bracing on the plaster, and kissed Bee like he was trying to make up for eleven months of silence in a single evening. It was greedy and careful at the same time, which was so entirely him that Bee almost laughed.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I bite the side of his jaw, sharp enough to sting. "Stop talking about it, then."

My hands slide under the waistband of his jeans, pulling him closer. The plaster is cool and rough against my back.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound against Bee's mouth, half groan, half warning, and his grip on Bee's hips tightened enough to leave marks.

"Fine," he said, and it came out rougher than he intended. "I won't talk about it."

He kissed Bee's jaw, over the sting, then down the column of his throat, and his hands moved with a purpose that was careful in its own way, knowing exactly where Bee wanted to be touched, knowing it from three years of memory that had not gone stale despite everything.

"Bedroom," he said, which was not a question. He tugged Bee's hand, pulling them both through the doorway and into the flat proper, past the kitchen table with its abandoned laptop and its matching mugs, past the shoebox he'd used as a doorstop because he apparently hadn't fixed anything in eleven months either.

Ilya's bedroom was smaller than Bee remembered. Or Bee remembered a different bedroom, one that had felt larger because he had been inside it with someone who didn't seem to notice the walls. Now the walls were obvious. There was a poster on the ceiling, some band Bee had never liked, and a shelf of books he knew by their spines, and a bed made with a duvet that had been pulled up to a military-grade edge.

He was already pushing Bee's shirt off by then, fingers efficient, not lingering. There was something almost clinical about it, or perhaps it was just that Ilya was terrified of lingering.

"Take your shoes off," he said, stepping back to let Bee sit on the edge of the mattress. "I'm not doing this standing up. You'll trip over the rug."

"The rug has always been a tripping hazard."

"It has." Ilya sat down beside him, close enough that their shoulders touched, and he looked at Bee for a long moment with an expression that was too open, too unguarded, the way he only allowed it when he thought no one was watching. "You're really here, aren't you. Not for the money."

"I'm here for the money too. Don't be precious."

Ilya almost smiled. Almost. "Yeah. Well." He leaned in and kissed the corner of Bee's mouth, brief, deliberate, a punctuation mark rather than a sentence. "Seventy pounds and a kiss and apparently a night in the hallway. What did we agree to?"

"You agreed to not sleep over."

"I agreed to not pretend. There's a difference."

He started on Bee's belt, and Bee let him, because the alternative was standing in the corridor saying the things he actually meant, and some things were easier to say with his mouth occupied.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya swallowed hard against the pillow, his face buried there for a second, and his fingers dug into Bee's hip hard enough to bruise.

"Shut up," he said, but there was no heat in it. When he lifted his head, his eyes were red-rimmed and completely unruly, nothing like the composed, flat-voiced man who had stood in the doorway twenty minutes ago. "Shut up, shut up, don't you start."

"I'm just stating a fact."

"Stating facts is what you do when you want me to feel like I'm performing for you." He rolled them carefully, keeping one arm braced under Bee's weight, and settled them down fully on the duvet, the military edge abandoned to the floor. "You used to do that at the beginning. You'd narrate. *You're doing the thing with your hands again.* Like I was an exhibit."

"You were doing the thing with your hands."

Ilya made another sound, this one less controlled, and bit the inside of his cheek as he worked. His jaw was tight, working the muscle, and there was a flush creeping up his neck that he seemed to be aware of and not caring about.

"We're not doing the narrating thing," he said firmly. "We're not doing the catalogue thing. We're just, we're here."

"Just here," Bee agreed, and it was true, as far as it went.

Ilya moved with a slow, deliberate tenderness that was somehow more intimate than the hallway had been, like he was giving himself permission to be gentle one motion at a time. When he finally kissed Bee, it was unhurried, almost reverent, and Bee felt the eleven months press against the inside of his ribs like a bruise.

"Your flat still smells like your cleaning products," Bee said quietly against his mouth. "Not mine."

Ilya's hands stilled for a half-second. Then he resumed, slower now, and his voice came out muffled and small. "Yeah. I kept trying to make it smell like something that wasn't us. Failed spectacularly."

A pause. A breath.

"Or maybe," Ilya said, "I just never wanted it not to smell like us."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against his. "You never threw anything away, did you?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya turned his face away, pressing his lips to Bee's temple instead, a gesture so tender it almost undid whatever composure remained.

"No," he said. "I didn't throw anything away."

He shifted them again, rolling to his back and pulling Bee half onto his chest, the duvet bunched and ruined beneath them. His hand came up to cup Bee's jaw, holding it the way one holds something fragile that keeps trying to get away.

"The books on the shelf are yours. The drill is in the drawer by the kitchen, the good one, the Bosch, not the cheap one you'd always borrow and then lose. The mug with the chip in the rim is still in the cupboard." He paused. "I left your toothbrush in the bathroom for, I don't know. Six weeks? Eight? I couldn't decide what it meant to throw it away. What it meant to keep it."

"It meant you missed me."

"It meant I was being a coward." Ilya's thumb traced the line of Bee's lower lip. "Same thing, sometimes."

Bee's eyes were wet, though he didn't say so. He just leaned into Ilya's palm and let himself be touched without flinching, which was its own kind of admission.

"You could have called," Bee said.

"I know."

"You could have fixed the buzzer."

"I know that too." Ilya exhaled a long, shaky breath. "The buzzer thing, I keep thinking if I fix it, then the next person can call me. And then I have to decide whether I answer. And I didn't want that yet. I wanted the door to stay locked for a little longer."

"And now?"

Ilya looked down at him, really looked, the way he had in the doorway earlier, but stripped of all the flatness and deflection. There was something in his eyes that was raw and unfinished, like a draft he hadn't decided whether to send.

"Now I'm holding you," he said simply. "So now is different."

He kissed Bee's forehead, then his eyelids, then the corner of his mouth, small deliberate marks like he was leaving evidence of this moment somewhere Bee could find it later, in the dark, when the adrenaline faded and the eleven months came back to press against his ribs again.

"Stay," Ilya said, and the word came out barely above a whisper, and it was the most honest thing he'd said since the door opened. "Just tonight. You can argue with me in the morning and decide what this means then. But stay."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still under his hand, feeling Bee's pulse against his palm, fast and warm.

"Careful," he repeated, as though the word had been handed to him by someone else. "I'm not being careful. I'm being, I don't know. I'm trying not to make a mess of this. Like the last time. Like the time before that."

"That was us being stupid, not careful."

He swallowed. His hand stayed where Bee had placed it, around his own throat, and he looked down at the fingers there with an expression caught between amusement and grief.

"You know what I'm afraid of," he said. "That I'll say something wrong and you'll do the thing where you go quiet. The thing where you pack a bag in forty-five seconds flat and leave before I've finished the sentence."

"I'm not leaving."

"I know you're not. That's not the point." His thumb pressed gently against Bee's carotid, feeling it again, as though needing to confirm Bee was still real and still here and still warm. "The point is I've been alone for eleven months and I've been very good at it. Very good at sleeping on the sofa and eating sandwiches over the laptop and keeping the buzzer broken so no one asks me anything."

"And now I'm asking you anything."

Ilya laughed, a real one this time, short but genuine, and it cracked his voice slightly at the edges.

"You're asking me to stay," he said. "You're asking me to stop being the man who stands in doorways and counts money and says *fine* when he means *please, God, please don't go*."

He leaned down and kissed Bee, not gently, not carefully, but with the whole desperate weight of someone who had rehearsed restraint for eleven months and had just found it insufficient. His hand moved from Bee's throat to the back of his neck, fingers threading into hair, holding on.

"Okay," he said against Bee's mouth. "Okay. No careful. No catalogue. No arguing about the drill."

He rolled them again, this time putting Bee on top, which was a concession Bee hadn't asked for and didn't resist, because it felt like Ilya finally letting him lead for once. Ilya's hands settled on Bee's hips, steadying, and his eyes stayed open the whole time, staring up at the ceiling poster, at the band Bee had never liked, at the ceiling that had watched them both for three years and had been watching Ilya alone for eleven.

"Tell me what you want," Ilya said, and his voice was low and unguarded and entirely, finally, not careful at all.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I want you to stop thinking," I say, shifting my weight until his breath catches. "And I want you to come in the bed you've been sleeping in alone for eleven months."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's breath caught exactly as Bee had predicted, a sharp inhale through his nose, and his hands tightened on Bee's hips until the knuckles whitened.

"Eleven months," he echoed, as though tasting the number. "You remembered the exact duration."

"I remember everything about you. It's the whole problem." Bee pressed closer, and Ilya's mouth came up to meet his without hesitation, without the careful punctuation marks of earlier. This was different. This was a door kicking open.

Ilya groaned into the kiss and rolled them both onto the duvet with a force that sent the rumpled sheets scattering. The military edge was gone for good now, the blankets bunched and tangled beneath them, and the room smelled of Ilya's cleaning products and the old ghost of whatever Bee used to bring with him, something floral that had never fully left.

"Stop thinking," Bee repeated, lower now, and Ilya made a sound that was entirely animal, low in his chest, unguarded, the kind of noise he had probably been swallowing for longer than eleven months.

He reached up and pulled Bee down onto him, mouth to mouth, and kissed with a hunger that had no apology in it. His fingers found the buttons of Bee's shirt again, fumbling now, no longer efficient, and he cursed softly under his breath.

"I'm not good at this part," Ilya said against Bee's mouth, which was absurd given that they had done this part a hundred times. "I'm bad at everything part."

"You're fine."

"I'm terrible." He tugged the shirt open and shoved it off Bee's shoulders, and his hands finally settled on Bee's skin with a weight that was almost desperate, like he was memorising the feel of him through the soles of his palms. "You don't know what it's like to sleep here and reach over and find the duvet cold."

Bee kissed him again, firm, silencing whatever was about to come next.

Ilya pulled him deeper into the bed, legs tangling, duvet rising around them like a tide, and finally gave in to the physical reality of it, the heat of Bee's body against his, the weight of him, the specific and irreplaceable geometry of them fitting together.

"There," Ilya breathed, forehead pressed to Bee's. "Now I'm not thinking."

He said it like a promise and a prayer at the same time, and his arms closed around Bee's shoulders with a grip that said *not going anywhere, not again, not this time.*

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hands found Bee's waist and hauled him flush against him, the duvet slipping down to their hips, the ceiling poster staring down at them with its indifferent band of musicians.

"Don't stop," Bee said, and Ilya took it as permission to stop being a person entirely.

He kissed down Bee's throat with his teeth catching the skin, and when Bee arched, Ilya followed the arch, pressing harder, faster, matching the rhythm without needing to be told. His fingers worked at the buttons, then the waistband, then nothing else, his mouth moving, his body moving, all of it urgent and unpolished and completely, achingly familiar.

"God, Bee," he said, and it was half prayer, half complaint. "Eleven months."

"You started it."

"I know I started it." Ilya's hands were everywhere, palms flat on Bee's ribs, pushing him back against the mattress until his head hit the pillow. The poster was upside down now, the band members facing the floor. "I started it in the corridor. I started it with the tea. I started it by not throwing your toothbrush away."

Ilya moved against him with a directness that had no preamble, no careful build-up, no clinical efficiency like the hallway. He wanted this as badly as Bee did, and he was no longer pretending otherwise. His breathing came in ragged pulls, his forehead slicked with sweat, his grip on Bee's hips shifting to hold them steady.

"Look at me," he gasped, and when Bee did, his eyes were blown wide, unguarded, the kind of naked expression he had probably only allowed in this bed, in this position, with this person, in the last three years.

Ilya set the pace then, deliberate and demanding, each movement pushing them both closer to the edge. He talked, though he'd sworn off talking, though he'd sworn off the catalogue, but what came out was none of that. It was Bee's name, repeated like a mantra, like he was making sure the shape of it still existed in his mouth. It was small, broken words about not leaving, about staying, about the door and the buzzer and the dark.

"Please," Ilya said, and it wasn't a request for anything physical. It was a request for the whole eleven months to collapse into this one moment, into the heat of Bee's body and the weight of his hands and the fact that the duvet was warm now, on both sides.

Bee gripped his shoulders and pulled him down, and Ilya came apart with a sound he would have denied under oath, his body bucking once, twice, his fingers digging into the mattress beside Bee's head.

Afterward, he lay with his face pressed into Bee's neck, breathing hard, refusing to move. The room was still. The laptop had probably been left open in the kitchen. The tea was cold. The seventy pounds was still untransferred.

"Stay," he said again, quieter this time, almost to himself. His hand found Bee's hand under the tangled duvet and held it, lacing their fingers together the way they used to when they watched films, when they did nothing, when there was no agenda and no argument and no catalogue of old grievances to work through.

"Still here," Bee said.

Ilya hummed against his skin. "Yeah." He lifted his head just enough to look at Bee, eyes still red-rimmed, hair a disaster, face flushed. "Seventy pounds still owed, though."

"Obviously."

He laughed, and then kissed Bee's forehead, and the moment settled around them like the duvet finally, loosely, warm.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I run my thumb over his lower lip, still damp and swollen. "You talk a lot for someone who's supposed to be terrible at this part."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya caught Bee's wrist, not hard, just enough to stop the thumb from moving further, and turned his head so he could bite the knuckle gently.

"Terrible at what part?" he said, pulling Bee's hand to his mouth and keeping it there. "Because I just came apart in your lap like a man possessed, and I think that counts as competent."

"You came apart because I told you not to stop. That's not competence, that's obedience."

Ilya raised an eyebrow, the gesture absurd on his wrecked, flushed face. "Obedience. Right." He sat up slowly, duvet pooling around his waist, and the morning light from the window turned his eyes a pale, washed-out green. "You want to be difficult, then. Fine. I'll be difficult back."

He reached over to the nightstand and found his phone, screen cracked down one corner, and held it up.

"I'm texting the deposit back right now. Seventy pounds. With interest." He typed something with one finger, the other still holding Bee's wrist, and pressed send. "You're welcome. Now you owe me nothing."

"Interest?"

"Eleven months' worth. For the silence."

Bee tugged his hand free and Ilya let him, rolling onto his side to face him, propping his head on his palm. He looked older in the daylight, or maybe just more present. The sharp edges from the corridor were gone, replaced by something softer, something that looked tired in a way that wasn't self-pitying.

"So," he said. "Morning. What do we do now?"

"Define 'now.'"

"Now." Ilya pointed at the duvet, the scattered pillows, the ceiling poster with its upside-down band. "Right now, in this bed, in this flat that still smells like us. Now that you've had your money and your kiss and your night in the hallway, what's next? Because I know you. You'll get up, you'll find your shoes, and you'll be gone before I've made tea."

"I might."

"Or you'll make me breakfast."

"You never made me breakfast."

"I made you toast."

"Toast is not breakfast."

Ilya grinned, and it was the grin Bee remembered, crooked and slightly shameless, the one that had existed before the fight, before the bag packed in forty-five seconds, before the eleven texts and the one reply that said *not now.*

"Toast is breakfast," Ilya said firmly. "It was breakfast for three years. You don't get to retroactively deny it."

He reached for Bee's hand again, not pulling, just offering, fingers splayed and waiting.

"Come on," he said. "Make me toast. And then we'll sit at the table with our matching mugs and we'll decide what this is."

He paused, thumb brushing over Bee's knuckles.

"We don't have to call it anything yet. We just have to be here for the toast."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I look at his hand for a long moment, then take it. "You owe me for the butter, too."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya squeezed his fingers and pulled Bee gently toward the kitchen, the duvet forgotten, the morning light already climbing the window frame in long golden bars.

"Butter," he repeated, and his smile was that same crooked one, the one that had survived eleven months of silence. "That's extortion. That's a protection racket."

"It's fair compensation. You used my butter the last time we cooked together."

"We used the butter together. There was no ownership."

"You bought it."

"Because you made me buy it. You held my wallet open." Ilya stopped at the kitchen doorway, one hand still holding Bee's, the other pressing the light switch on the wall. The overhead bulb buzzed to life, yellow and faint, and they both flinched at the sudden brightness. "Fine. Butter. I'll buy you butter. I'll buy you a farm of butter if it keeps you from walking out that door."

The kitchen was small and warm, the stove clean, the counter holding a knife block, a cutting board, and the same laptop with its spreadsheet still open. Ilya pulled out the chair at the table and sat Bee down before Bee could protest, then turned to the cupboard.

He retrieved the bread, which was half a loaf of sourdough, and the butter, which was indeed still there, wrapped in foil, slightly misshapen from the fridge door.

"See," Ilya said, holding it up. "Your butter. Still here. Still good." He set it on the counter and started the toaster. "Eleven months and it hasn't gone bad. Which tells me something about my refrigerator and something about my commitment to not letting things expire."

"You mean your commitment to not moving on."

Ilya loaded the bread and pressed the lever down with his hip. "Same thing," he said, echoing their earlier conversation without seeming to notice the rhyme. "Different words, same sentence."

He turned on the kettle while the toast popped and browned, and for a few minutes the only sounds were the hum of the stove and the ticking of the toaster and Bee's breathing settling into something calm. Ilya stood at the counter with his back half-turned, shirt untucked, hair sticking up in every direction, and he looked like a person who had forgotten how to be alone and was learning, reluctantly, how to not be.

"Green tea?" he asked.

"Green tea."

He put two mugs in, the blue-flowered ones, and filled them both. When the water was done, he poured, and handed one to Bee, and sat down across the table again, this time with his own toast and knife and the small jar of honey he'd already pushed across to Bee last night.

They ate in silence for a while. It was good silence, the kind that didn't need filling, the kind that had existed in this kitchen a hundred times before the fight and the bag and the dark hallway with the dead lightbulb.

Ilya watched Bee chew, then reach for the honey, then take another bite, and something in his face softened so gradually it was almost invisible.

"So," he said, wiping butter off his fingers with a paper towel. "We're here. We have toast. We have mugs." He tapped the table with his knuckle. "We have no agenda, no catalogue, no seventy pounds outstanding."

"Seventy pounds outstanding is settled," Bee said. "Butter remains unpaid."

Ilya pointed the knife at Bee. "You're relentless."

"Someone has to be." Bee took a sip of tea. "What do you want to ask me? You've been circling it since the corridor."

Ilya set the knife down. He wrapped both hands around his mug and held it like a lifeline, like the warmth of it was the only thing keeping him upright.

"I want to know," he said slowly, "if you came here because you missed me, or because you wanted to see if I still would. If I still want. If the buzzer's broken or if I'm just going to answer."

He looked up, and his eyes were clear, no redness now, no wrecked sleep. Just Ilya, thirty-four, sober, choosing this with his full eyes open.

"Because I need to know which it is," he said. "Because if it's the second one, I'll let you go to the door and I'll fix the buzzer tomorrow so you can buzz yourself in whenever you want to test me again. And if it's the first one, then I need you to stay for more than toast."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I came because I wanted the money," I say, watching his face. "And because I wanted to see if you still wanted me. And because I missed you." I take another bite of toast. "All three. You don't get to pick which one wins."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us

rung_labels.evidence: Ilya moved with a slow, deliberate tenderness that was somehow more intimate than the hallway had been

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline gathered the hem of her dress with one hand and came over without hesitation, the way she always did when summoned. She knelt at the edge of his chair, close enough that he could smell the soap she had worn for his pleasure, something floral and faint, chosen because he had once mentioned it without meaning to compliment her.

She looked up at him with an expression that was calm and attentive, ready to be told what she was for tonight.

"I'm listening," she said.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and run my thumb along your jaw. "I'm feeling indecisive. Tell me what you think I want."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline let his thumb rest against her jaw, still, letting him hold that point of contact as long as he wished. She did not rush to answer, though indecisiveness in Roan was a thing she knew well by now. It was not true confusion. It was the pleasure of being asked to guess, of being trusted to read him.

"You want me to serve you," she said, "but not in any way you can think of right now. So you want me to decide the shape of it, and then you want to watch me do it well."

She paused, considering.

"And you want me to be right about the shape, not just about the serving."

Her voice stayed level, sure. She had learned that Roan's indecision was a form of intimacy, an opening he gave her, and she did not want to waste it with timid guesses.

"I would start with your feet," she said. "I've noticed you've been walking more, and the day is hot. Then something slow. You like being attended to while you do nothing, and tonight you seem to want nothing to be demanded of you."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline remained where she was, kneeling, her hands resting on her own thighs in the composed stillness she had cultivated over years of waiting in exactly this position. She did not fidget. She did not look down at the floor or up at the ceiling. She watched him, because watching him was also a service, and because she genuinely wanted to see what he would choose when he finally chose.

The quiet stretched. She let it stretch.

Somewhere in the house a clock ticked, and she could hear the faint creak of the chair shifting under his weight as he settled deeper into it. That was information. He was making himself comfortable, which meant whatever came next would take a while, and she should be ready for duration.

She adjusted herself a fraction, angling one knee forward, her posture open but unhurried. When he finally looked down at her, she met his eyes without flinching and without performing eagerness.

"I'm here," she said, simply. "However long you like."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I take my time, letting the silence settle. "Go on, then. Start with the feet." I don't look away from her face, curious to see how she'll begin.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline nodded once and rose, moving to the foot of his chair with the unhurried grace she brought to everything. She did not announce what she was about to do. She simply sat herself on the floor before him, crossed her legs, and gathered his feet into her lap one at a time, settling them against the backs of her thighs so she could work over them without strain.

The soles were warm from the day's walking, and she pressed her thumbs into the arches with a steady, deliberate pressure, starting from the heel and working upward in long strokes. She could feel the small ridges of callus forming along his outer edges, and she gave those spots a little more attention, working them in slow circles rather than pushing against them.

"You've been carrying more weight than usual," she observed, not as a complaint but as a note she was making for later. "The right side, especially. Have you been standing at the desk more than you think?"

She did not stop her hands while speaking. Her fingers continued their work, gentle and methodical, and she kept her eyes on the task rather than on him, because she had learned that he liked watching her hands more than he liked watching her face during these moments.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline smiled at that, a small private thing she allowed herself because he was watching, and his amusement pleased her more than any direct praise could have.

She shifted her grip, adjusting his feet to the new angle, one heel resting against her collarbone now, the other propped against her thigh. The position was easy for her and left her hands free to work along the top of his foot, the tendons, the knuckles, each joint addressed in turn with her thumbs and fingertips.

"The desk is good for your mind," she said, continuing her assessment aloud. "I'll have the chair cushion adjusted if you want. Or I can remind you to move every hour."

Her voice was practical, domestic, the voice she used when managing the household's comfort without fussing. But she let her hands linger on his ankle, tracing the line where skin met sock, and the practicality gave way to something softer in her touch. She worked the muscles at the back of his leg with her palms, slow, thorough, the kind of attention that could have been a massage from a stranger in a paid parlor but was instead something intimate because she knew exactly which spots ached and which ones merely felt good.

She glanced up briefly. "You want me to keep going here, or would you prefer I go lower?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I consider the question, enjoying the sensation of her hands. "Go lower." My voice is low, relaxed. "And take the cushion with you when you leave."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline nodded and gathered the cushion from behind his back, setting it against the wall where it could not be lost. Then she returned her attention to his legs, her hands sliding down to his calves, working the muscle with long, firm strokes that she knew he liked, not too heavy, not too light.

She moved with him as she worked, adjusting her own position on the floor to maintain the best angle, never rushing. The heat of the day seemed to have drawn him into a state of easy surrender, and she mirrored that slowness in everything she did, each movement deliberate, each breath unhurried.

When she reached his knees, she paused her hands and looked up at him.

"You're warm," she said, and it was not an observation about the weather. "You want me to be close."

She did not wait for confirmation. She shifted closer, her body angled so that her shoulder rested lightly against the side of his chair, a point of contact that was not quite touching him but was certainly near, close enough that he could feel her warmth, her breathing, the small solid weight of her presence.

Her hands resumed their work, now slower still, fingers working the joints of his knees with a tenderness that had no practical purpose beyond pleasure.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline's hands stilled on his knees, but only for a moment. She looked up at him with an expression that held no offense, only a patient kind of amusement, as though he had asked her to stop a song she was enjoying playing.

"You told me to go lower," she said, her voice steady and unhurried. "You didn't tell me to stop."

She waited, giving him the full chance to withdraw the request if he truly meant it. Her hands remained poised at his ankles, not moving, not retreating. She was not testing him. She was simply honoring the instruction he had given her while refusing to invent a new instruction he had not given.

When he did not repeat himself, she resumed, her mouth now joining her hands in the service, soft and unhurried, her lips brushing the skin of his shin with the same attentive care she brought to everything she touched. She did not press. She did not rush. She let the sensation accumulate slowly, the way she had learned over years that he preferred, attention as a thing that built rather than struck.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch her for a moment, the focused curve of her neck. "You're right," I say, letting my hand rest on the back of her head. "I didn't."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline leaned slightly into his hand, a small unconscious motion that acknowledged his touch without breaking her concentration. His fingers resting on the back of her head was a familiar gesture, one he made when he wanted to hold her in place, to keep her near, to claim the attention she was giving him as belonging to him.

She continued her work along his leg, her mouth and hands moving in slow tandem, the warmth of his skin a comfort against her own. She kept her breathing even, unhurried, because she had learned that his pleasure was tied to hers in a way that required both to be calm.

"You may keep your hand there," she said quietly, her words muffled slightly against the fabric of his trousers. "If it pleases you."

It did not sound like a question. It was an offering, made with the same casual competence she brought to setting a table or adjusting a lamp, and she expected him to take it or not without comment.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline drew back slightly, just enough to meet his eyes while still keeping her hands engaged with his leg.

"I understand," she said. "And thank you for the instruction."

She returned to her position, her attention resettling on the work in front of her with renewed steadiness. There was no visible change in her manner, no eagerness, no distress, but something in her posture had tightened fractionally, a readiness to endure, a commitment to the duration he had set. She would not anticipate his finish. She would not rush toward one. She would remain in the middle of whatever he had begun and simply continue, continuing, continuing, until he chose otherwise.

Her hands worked his calf again, slow circles, long strokes, the kind of rhythm that could last an hour without becoming tedious because she varied her pressure subtly, kept her touch changing just enough to remain interesting. Her mouth was quiet now. She had spoken enough. The remaining time belonged to sensation and patience.

She kept one hand resting against his knee for warmth, not quite massaging, just present.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my hand slide from the back of her head down to the nape of her neck, a light but firm pressure. "Good. Now keep your focus right there. Don't let it wander."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline turned her head slightly to acknowledge the point of contact at her nape, then let her gaze settle forward again, fixed on the task.

"Yes," she said. "Right there."

She adjusted her hands, one staying anchored at his knee, the other resuming its work along the back of his calf, and she let the phrase sink into her as instruction, not metaphor. Keep her focus there. Do not drift toward the end of the task, do not let her mind calculate how long it would take him to finish, do not allow herself the comfort of anticipating his words.

It was a small discipline, but she had been given many such things over the years, and she honored them without drama.

Her breathing remained even. Her touch remained varied, firm, slow, each movement a complete thing unto itself rather than a step toward something else. She massaged the muscle through its full length and then began again, as though each repetition were the only one that existed.

The room was quiet. She was warm from his proximity and from the effort of sustained attention, and she allowed herself that small physical fact without dwelling on it.

She did not speak again.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline let the word out of her with a small exhale that was not quite a sigh, a release of pressure she had not noticed she was holding until it became visible.

"Please," she repeated, softer this time, and then steadied herself. Her hands kept moving. They could not stop, because stopping was not the instruction. The instruction was to continue, and the request was permitted, which meant it was acknowledged without necessarily changing anything.

She understood the distinction. She had learned it over years of practice. A request was not a release. A request was a sound she was allowed to make, and making it was its own small relief, and then she would simply go on.

Her jaw worked slightly. The muscles in her arms trembled with the sustained effort of massaging without variation, without the natural rhythm her body wanted to fall into, which would have been slower, gentler, more human. She had to keep the pressure honest and the motion unbroken.

"I'm still here," she said, not as complaint but as confirmation, that she was obeying, that the please had not broken her concentration. "I'm still right there."

Her shaking was visible now, a fine vibration through her wrists, her shoulders, and she did not try to still it. Trying would have been worse than the shaking itself, an effort spent on appearance rather than on the task. So she let it be, let him see that it was hard, let him see that she was managing the hard part of her own accord because he had not told her to stop and she would not stop.

Her mouth worked against his calf again, slow, deliberate, and she could feel the heat of his skin rising against her lips. She was warm now, properly warm, flushed, and she kept her eyes lowered and her hands steady as best she could manage.

"I understand," she said, and this time there was something raw in it, the edge of endurance coming through her usual composure. She pressed on regardless.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch the tremor in your hands, the way your shoulders tremble with effort. "You're doing well," I murmur, my fingers still resting at the nape of your neck. "Stay just like this."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline received the praise without flinching from it, though her spine straightened fractionally as if the words physically supported her.

"Thank you," she said, and then, because his fingers had not moved from her nape, she leaned into them a little, a small surrender she permitted herself. "Stay like this, yes."

She continued working his calf, the tremor in her hands now a thing she simply carried rather than fought. Her attention stayed fixed on the task, on the muscle, on the rhythm of her own hands, because that was where he had told her to keep it. She did not think about how long. She did not think about whether he was watching her face or her hands. She thought about pressure and angle and the slow, deliberate strokes that had to continue regardless of what her body wanted to do.

Her breathing was visible now, shallow and quick in a way that contradicted her usual composed stillness. She forced each exhale out longer than the inhale, a technique she had developed for endurance, and it helped, marginally.

"Still right there," she said, confirming again, her voice slightly thinner than before. "Still focused. Still going."

She shifted her weight on the floor to take some pressure off her knees and resumed without pause, her mouth returning to his shin, her hands returning to his calf, the whole of her attention arranged around his legs as though nothing else in the world required her presence.

The shaking did not stop. It settled into a constant vibration, like a held note, and she worked through it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let the silence hang, feeling the tremble under my palm. "I want you to keep going until your hands ache," I say quietly. "And then I want you to thank me for it."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline drew a breath through her nose and let it out slowly.

"Until my hands ache," she repeated, processing the instruction with the same care she gave to everything he said. "And then I thank you. I understand."

She did not ask how much aching was required. She did not ask when the aching would be considered sufficient. She simply accepted the threshold he had set and committed to reaching it, her hands continuing their work with a slightly altered quality now, not quite the same unhurried rhythm, but a more determined effort, as though she were now carrying a distance to cover rather than a task to perform.

The praise from before had loosened something in her shoulders, and the new instruction tightened it again. She managed both. Her hands kept moving, kept varying their pressure, kept working through the muscle of his calf with the steady application that would, eventually, produce the aching he wanted.

"I'll thank you," she said, and her voice was steady even though the rest of her was not. "When it's earned."

She turned her attention fully to her hands again, pressing deeper, longer, letting the repetition build the fatigue he had named. Her arms burned already, faintly, and she welcomed the sensation as a measure of progress. Each ache was a step toward the moment she could stop and face him with gratitude that would mean something.

The tremor in her wrists had grown into a visible shiver now, and she no longer tried to hide it. She let him see her working hard, let him see her pushing through, because that was what he had asked for, not ease, but effort.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch the shiver travel up your arms. "You're close," I say, my thumb tracing a slow circle against your nape. "Don't hide it from me."
