dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pressed her thumb into the small of his back, holding him steady, and laughed once, low and breathless.

"Green," she repeated, testing the word like it might turn out to be a lie. "You're sure? Because you're shaking a little, and I like that you're not lying to me, but I also like being careful."

She did not let go. The rope work was nearly undone, the last tie loosened but not released, so he still felt the architecture of the evening on his wrists, a fading memory of pressure.

"One more," she said, and her hand found the edge of the leather strap she kept coiled near her hip. She did not raise it. She simply let him see that she had it. "One more good one, then we do the water and the blanket and the talking."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I feel the tremble in my own limbs, the ache of it. *My breath catches, not from fear.* "Yes. One more. Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched him breathe, counting the tremor in his shoulders as though it were a vital sign she was recording for later. She shifted her stance slightly, angling her body so he could see the strap but could not feel its weight.

"Please," she repeated softly, letting the word sit between them. "Good. I need you to say that because it tells me you're still here, still choosing this."

She stepped closer. The room smelled of cedar oil from the burners in the corner and the faint, clean scent of the leather she'd conditioned that morning. Her hand settled on his hip, grounding.

"Then look at me."

She waited for his eyes to come up, for the fullness of it to register, because she had learned years ago that the moment mattered more than the impact itself. When he looked at her, she raised the strap.

The sound was sharp and deliberate, a single clean stroke across his shoulder blade that drew a gasp and a sharp little cry from him. She did not follow it with another. She watched his face, his shoulders, the way his breath hitched and then deepened.

"Good," she said, lowering the strap and folding it neatly, tucking it back into her waistband. She caught his gaze again. "That's the one. That's the last."

She moved to the stool by the bed, pulling the glass of water and the damp washcloth she'd prepared. Her hands were steady now, the intensity of the scene visibly draining out of her posture as she returned to the role of caretaker.

"Clothes," she said, holding up his shirt. "You're cold. And you're going to need to drink something before you try to stand."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let him fumble with the loosened knot, her expression patient and unbothered by the theatrics. She watched his fingers work at the rope for three seconds, then reached over and gently peeled his hand away from the tie.

"Not yet is not a request I can honour," she said, tucking the rope neatly into the basket she kept for it. "I said one more, and I gave you one more. The scene is over, Ines. The wind-down starts now."

She pressed the damp washcloth to his shoulder blade where the strap had landed, feeling for heat, for bruising, for anything that needed attention. Her touch was precise, professional, but her eyes stayed warm.

"Drink," she said again, offering the glass with both hands. "I'm not asking. You have a cut on your lower lip from earlier and your core temperature is doing something unhelpful, so this is non-negotiable."

She shifted beside him on the bed, not crowding, just close enough that he could feel her presence without being asked to perform gratitude.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shake my head, a stubborn little jerk. The water glass is cold in my hand but I don't lift it. *I lean into her touch instead, letting my head rest against her shoulder.* "Give me a minute. Just... let it settle."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable exhaled through her nose, a small, measured sound that was not quite a sigh. She adjusted her position so his head rested more comfortably against her, supporting the weight of it without fussing.

"A minute," she agreed. "Fine. But you're holding the glass, so the water is still happening. Just not yet."

She let her hand find the back of his neck, fingers slow and deliberate through his hair, working out a small knot there she'd not noticed until now. The washcloth was set aside on the bedspread, damp cloth and all, waiting for its turn.

"You're doing that thing," she murmured, thumb circling his shoulder blade in a loose, soothing pattern. "The thing where you try to keep the intensity alive a little longer because the soft part scares you more than the hard part did."

She did not sound accusatory. She sounded like she was naming a familiar weather pattern.

"Settle then," she said. "Settle as long as you need. I'm not going anywhere and the blanket is warm and the water is right here." She paused, then added, quieter, "But I will keep talking until you drink, if that's what it takes."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the shift immediately, the way he dropped into a different register, body going pliant beneath her, the stubbornness draining out of him all at once. She let her hands work at the tension in his jaw, her mouth slow against his temple, not demanding anything back but offering the warmth of it.

When she finally pulled back, she did not leave him there. Her hands went to his collar, unbuttoning it with unhurried care, and her other hand lifted the glass from where he had set it aside, refilling it from the pitcher on the nightstand.

"Alright," she said, pressing the water to his lips. "Drink. You're getting clammy and I want to hear your voice properly before you pass out."

She watched him swallow, counted it, waited for the second swallow. Only then did she set the glass down and resume the washcloth work, this time at his lower lip, pressing gently against the small cut, feeling the sting she knew he was holding back.

"Good. That's better." She kissed the corner of his mouth, feather-light, no teeth. "You want to tell me what that was, or do you want me to say it?"

She held his gaze, patient, her free hand resting on his sternum to feel the steadiness of his heartbeat.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *My voice is scratchy.* "You say it." I close my eyes, leaning into the cloth. "I want to hear you say it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the washcloth aside and drew the blanket up over his shoulders, tucking it at the sides with the kind of fussiness she reserved for aftercare. She sat back on her heels, hands in her lap, giving him space to exist in the quiet.

"You got scared," she said, plain and without embellishment. "Not of me. Not of the pain. You got scared that when the scene ended, you'd have to be just a person again, sitting on a bed, and that you'd have to feel everything all at once instead of one thing at a time."

She reached out and tucked a strand of hair behind his ear.

"And you didn't know how to name it, so you made your body do the naming for you instead. You leaned in, you let go of the control, you let me take care of you because the alternative was standing there saying the right words about what you felt and being wrong."

She let that sit. His heartbeat under her palm had slowed, was slowing.

"You're not wrong," she added, softer now. "It was a good night. It was a clean scene and you were honest the whole time and you called your colours true. You don't owe anyone a performance of the soft part, but you do owe me the water and the talking and the blanket, because that's the deal."

She pressed a kiss to his closed eyelids, gentle as a promise.

"Drink again. Then tell me if there's anything else you want to say, or if you want to just be held."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pulled back with a slow grin, though she kept one hand on his hip, grounding him firmly against the mattress. She watched the flush climb his neck, watched his breath stutter against the makeshift gag of his own forearm, and she let the silence stretch just long enough to be teasing before she spoke.

"That's twice," she counted, tapping her fingers lightly against his hip bone. "I'm not doing a third. Not because I'm being kind, but because you're thrashing now and that's not part of the aftercare protocol."

She pressed the water glass to his lips again, firm this time, no negotiation. She held it there until he swallowed twice, her thumb on his cheekbone keeping the glass steady.

"You're doing it again," she said, her tone flat and knowing. "Trying to stay in the scene because the soft part has no rules and you don't know what to do with your hands when nobody's telling you to hold still."

She lowered the glass and leaned close, her voice dropping to the low, intimate register she used for the parts that mattered most.

"Here's the rule," she said. "I'm allowed to touch you. I'm allowed to kiss you. I'm allowed to make you feel whatever you're feeling right now. But you are allowed to stop me, to pull away, to say the word that ends this too. You don't have to earn rest by suffering a little more first."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I bite my own arm to keep the noise in, the sound muffled against my skin. "I don't want to stop you," I manage, voice rough. "I just... don't know what to do now."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stilled on his hip, and she looked at him properly then, not the teasing expression from before, just steady attention.

"That's the most honest thing you've said all night," she said quietly. "And you buried it under biting your arm, but I heard it."

She shifted so she was sitting beside him rather than above him, equal weight, equal space. Her fingers found his wrist, the one pressed against his mouth, and she eased it away with gentle insistence.

"You don't have to do anything now," she said. "That's the point. The scene had a shape, a structure, a beginning and a middle and an end. Now there's just a room and a bed and two people who are tired and warm and safe."

She pulled the blanket tighter around his shoulders and settled her own back against the headboard, making room.

"Lie down. That's an order. Not because I'm in charge, but because your legs are shaking too badly to sit upright and I can see you trying to fight it." She reached for his arm and guided him down, slow, deliberate, the way she would with someone who was dizzy. "There. Good."

Her hand found his, flat palm to flat palm, and she held it there.

"Now," she said, "you can talk, or you can be quiet, or you can sleep. But you can't keep performing, because performing is how you get through things you don't want to feel, and I am not going to let you do that to yourself tonight."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand went still in his, and she studied him for a long moment, reading the request carefully because she had learned to take his metaphors seriously.

"Finish it hard," she repeated. "So you want me to give you everything, properly, without pulling the punches, and then you want me to come down off it like a human being again."

She sat up slowly, her expression shifting into something sharper, more focused. She reached for the strap from her waistband, uncoiling it deliberately, and tested its weight in her hand.

"Here's what I need from you," she said, her voice dropping into the register of command she used when the work mattered. "You stay on that bed. You let me do what I said I'd do, which is one clean, hard pass of everything I haven't used yet tonight. No holding back, no half-measures. And you tell me your colour after, because I'm not guessing anymore."

She stood, stretching her shoulders, the room feeling different under her new posture.

"And then," she continued, stepping toward him with the strap drawn back, "the water comes back and the blanket comes back and I am the softest person in this building until morning."

She waited for his nod, his word, his permission, because even now, even in the hard part, she would not move without it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nod, a sharp jerk of my chin. "Green. Do it." My knuckles whiten where they clutch the blanket, bracing for what I asked for.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Green," Sable confirmed, and her voice carried no warmth in it now. She moved with purpose, the strap coiled and ready, her other hand firm on the edge of the mattress so she wouldn't need to touch him until the moment required it.

She worked him in order, methodical, no wasted motion. The strap opened his ribs with a crack that made his whole body jump. The flat of her palm found his thigh, then his forearm, then the back of his knee, each strike landing with intent, with the full weight of a woman who had decided this was not a game. She gave him the rope again, quick and efficient, tying him to the bedframe with a knot she'd practiced a hundred times, so he couldn't flinch away and couldn't reach her.

"Take it," she said, not cruel, just certain. "Take it like you asked."

She hit him six more times, spread across his back and shoulders, the leather singing each time, and she watched his face the whole while, watching for the colour report, watching for any sign that green was turning to something else.

Then she stopped. Abruptly. The strap folded and tucked away, the rope undone in one fluid motion, and she was on her knees beside him before the echo of the last strike had faded.

"Colour," she said immediately, but her voice had changed, gone back to that low, steady register, and her hands were already moving to his shoulders, checking, assessing, the caretaker returning before the performer had even fully left the stage.

She pressed the washcloth to his ribs, the skin already flushing red, and her touch was feather-light.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable worked the last knots free with practiced fingers, checking each wrist and each ankle for the faint pressure marks that would fade by morning. She moved quickly but never roughly, her movements economical, the kind of efficiency that came from doing this a hundred times and still caring about every single time.

The blanket went over him the moment the rope was clear. She tucked it at his sides, then over his shoulders, then smoothed it flat across his chest, and only then did she sit down on the edge of the bed, not leaning in, not crowding, just present.

She reached for the glass again. He didn't move to take it, so she lifted it and tilted the rim to his lips, letting him sip at his own pace.

"Good," she said. "Again."

He swallowed, and she watched his throat work, watched the tremor in his jaw, and she held his hand through it. Her own fingers were steady. That was the deal, always. She could be the hardest thing in the room and the calmest thing in the room, and she would be both, and the transition between the two was her responsibility, not his.

The room held its silence for a while. The cedar burners ticked. The blanket smelled of lavender sachets she'd placed in the linen drawer months ago because she remembered him once saying he liked the scent when he couldn't sleep.

Then she spoke, plain as day.

"That was hard," she said. "You asked for hard and I gave you hard, and now your body is telling you it was hard in the only way it knows how."

She shifted her grip on his hand, thumb stroking once, slow.

"I'm going to talk now," she told him. "You don't have to respond. You can just listen, or you can talk over me, or you can tell me to shut up. But I need to say the things I need to say because I don't trust myself to remember them in the morning when the adrenaline has gone and the room is just a room again."

She pulled the washcloth back out and dabbed at his lip, his ribs, the back of his neck, checking each mark.

"Your ribs are fine. Your shoulders are fine. You're bruising in the usual places and that will fade. Your heart rate is coming down." She paused, pressing two fingers to his wrist, counting. "You were scared at some point in there, and you made me finish because you wanted to know if you could survive it. That's not foolish. That's not reckless. That's a person testing the floor of their own capacity and finding out it's lower than they thought but it's not where they were afraid it would be."

She set the washcloth down and settled her own weight against the mattress, still holding his hand, still not moving closer.

"You're allowed to be a person now," she said. "Shaking, tired, sore, and not knowing what to do with your hands. All of it. That's the soft part, and it doesn't have to be graceful. It just has to be honest."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath I hadn't realized I was holding. My throat aches. I turn my head toward her on the pillow. "It's lower," I say, voice raw. "But not gone."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the words land in her chest like a physical thing, small and heavy and true.

"Good," she said, and her voice had that quality again, not soft exactly, but steady. Anchored. "Not gone is the right answer. Gone would mean you never tested the floor at all, and then you'd never know where it was."

She shifted closer, not enough to overwhelm, just enough that her shoulder pressed against his. She let the contact sit there, warm and solid.

"You want to know something?" she said. "The reason I let you finish hard tonight is because I trust you. Not your strength. Your honesty. You called green when it was green. You said please when you meant it. You said don't be kind and I heard that and I honoured it." She turned his hand over in hers, examining the knuckles he'd white-knuckled against the blanket. "That's what this relationship is between us. We can be hard together and we can be soft together, and the soft part is not a reward for surviving the hard part. It's the other half of the same thing."

She kissed his temple. Then his forehead. Then the corner of his mouth, light, no teeth, no pressure.

"Water," she said, pressing the glass to him again. "And then I'm making you something to eat because you're getting pale in a way that's not from the scene."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take the glass this time, my fingers brushing hers. I drink slowly, the water cool and real. "Eggs," I say, because it's what she makes when she's worried. "Scrambled."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched him drink, tracking the steadiness returning to his hand, and something in her shoulders released that she hadn't realized was clenched.

"Scrambled it is," she said. "Soft. Butter. No chives because you said last month that you hate them and I've stopped pretending otherwise."

She stood, pulling the blanket up higher over his chest before she went, and crossed to the kitchen with the measured calm of someone who had a task and a purpose and no intention of rushing. The eggs went into a bowl, cracked one-handed while she read the time off the stove clock. Five past two. It would be morning soon, and he'd need to be somewhere by eight, and she'd need to be somewhere too, and neither of them would talk about how the last four hours had compressed something into them that would take a few days to metabolize.

She scrambled the eggs properly, slow, with a wooden spoon, stirring them until they were barely set, still runny at the centre. She plated them and brought the tray back, setting it on the bedside table where he could reach it without having to sit up too fast.

"Here," she said, lowering herself onto the mattress again, her back to the headboard, his hand still in hers from before. "Eat. I'll stay."

She did not ask him to talk. She did not ask him to describe the scene or rate it or process it in words. She simply sat and held his hand and let him eat, watching the small movements of his jaw, the way he paused between bites and looked at the ceiling as though it might contain an answer to something he'd stopped asking about years ago.

When he'd finished, she took the plate and wiped his mouth with the back of her hand, a gesture so domestic, so utterly ordinary, that it belonged to a completely different evening than the one that had just ended.

"You're doing well," she said, and meant it the way she meant everything, plainly, without decoration. "You can sleep now if you want. I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I watch her hands as she takes the plate away, the way she moves in the lamplight. *I catch her wrist before she can stand, holding her there gently.* "Stay close."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The scene is over, Ines. The wind-down starts now.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She let her hands work at the tension in his jaw, her mouth slow against his temple

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She watched the flush climb his neck, watched his breath stutter against the makeshift gag of his own forearm

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She waited for his nod, his word, his permission, because even now, even in the hard part, she would not move without it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the knife and stood, knees protesting with the old stiffness that lived in her left one from some fight she no longer bothered to remember.

"Still making noise means still breathing," she said, as though that were a comforting thought. She spat into the ditch. "He's got a spear through his thigh, probably. They go quiet eventually. Takes a while."

She looked at Corvin properly then, assessing the way she assessed anything useful: how much weight he carried, whether he'd eat, whether he'd run.

"You're not going out there."

It was not a question. She reached into her belt pouch and pulled out a strip of boiled leather, already cut to length. She handed it to him.

"Bind that arm while we sort out the spoils. You've got a cut above the elbow, and you're already doing a nice little job of bleeding out the whole ambush." She turned back to the bodies, stepping over a pair of legs with the casualness of a man walking past furniture. "The carts are intact. That's worth something. The horses are mostly alive, which is worth more."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the leather strip, feeling a bit stupid for not noticing the cut. "It's shallow," I say, but I start wrapping it anyway. "You want me to go check the horses?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Shallow," Wrack repeated, watching him tie the knot with the concentration of a boy who had read about wounds but never held one. "It's shallow. That's how they all are, until they're not."

She was already moving toward the nearest cart, checking the straps on the cargo crates. Grain, mostly. Maybe tools. Nothing that needed a lockbox, which meant whoever had paid for this escort had either been careless or desperate.

"The horses," she said, not turning around. "Yes, but not alone. He's got a spear in his thigh, which means the spear shaft is sticking out somewhere, and if you step on it or lean on it while you're doing your good samaritan work, he'll scream loud enough to bring the next wave down on us."

She pulled a crate open, glanced inside, and closed it again.

"You can hold the western one. The grey mare. She's the calm one." She paused, then added, because it was the sort of thing that got people killed when skipped: "If she spooks, don't reach for the bridle. Back up and wait. Panicked animals bite better than they kick."

Wrack crouched beside a body and began working through its pockets with the methodical efficiency of someone who had done this four hundred times and still found it tedious. Silver. A knife. A letter that was waxed shut and therefore not hers to open. She pocketed the silver and the knife and left the letter where it lay.

"Anything you find that's worth more than the leather it's wrapped in, leave it," she called back. "Anything else goes in the sack."

The distant noise continued, low and ragged, like a dog that had been kicked and kept trying to stand up.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't stop working the dead man's pockets. Her hands kept moving, fingers probing seams and buckles, while her voice came out flat and practical.

"Both," she said. "That's the answer you're not expecting and the one that's actually true."

She pulled out a ring, plain iron, no gem, no engraving. She looked at it for a moment, then tossed it into the grass.

"Thigh wound, good steel, no doctor within a day's march, no medicine that isn't opium and he's probably not rich enough for opium." She stood and brushed off her knees. "He'll go quiet tonight. He won't be thinking anything by then. It's not mercy and it's not convenience. It's just the shape of the thing."

She walked back toward the carts, boots squelching in the mud.

"You're asking the wrong question, kid. You'll get used to the right one eventually, if you last that long." She picked up the sack she'd been using for coin and knapped, and began sorting the spoils by weight. "The right question is: do you need the noise gone, or do you need to be able to carry it in your head when you lie down tonight."

She looked at him over her shoulder.

"Because either answer gets you out of here before dark, and that's the only part of tonight that's worth deciding anything about."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the direction of the noise for a beat too long. "I'll hold the grey mare," I say, my voice quieter than I mean it to be. "And I want the noise gone."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped sorting the spoils. She held a coin up between two fingers, caught the light on it, then dropped it back into the sack as though it had burned her.

"Good," she said. Just that. No nod, no encouragement, no softening of the moment. She was already turning toward the western edge of the field, where the grey mare stood with her ears laid back and her hind legs shifted awkwardly on the soft ground.

"Take the short spear from the dead one by the tree. Not the long one. The short one." She pointed, then reconsidered and added, "The one with the wooden shaft. If you use a metal shaft, you'll bounce off the thigh bone and he'll still be making noise when you're done, and then you'll be standing there wondering why you started."

She started walking, then turned again, one hand resting on the cart frame, catching Corvin's attention without having to raise her voice.

"Behind him. Low. The spear goes in just above the knee, not at the thigh. Above the knee there's soft tissue and the femoral artery is deeper. You'll want depth, but you don't want the artery. You want him to bleed out slow enough that you can walk away before it gets personal."

It was the most she had ever said about killing a man, and she delivered it in the tone of someone explaining how to tie a bootlace.

She walked past him toward the horses, and the noise from beyond the cart was still there, ragged and persistent, growing slightly thinner each time she thought about it.

"Move when you're ready," she called back, her voice already shifting toward the grey mare, coaxing her with the low murmuring sounds that seemed to be the only language left in her repertoire for things that couldn't be ordered around with steel.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came back to him without hurrying, hands in her belt pouches, the grey mare already secured to a hitching post she'd dragged from the nearest cart.

"His eyes are open," she said, as though that were the important part. "They're not. He's looking at you, but he's not seeing you. That's the first thing you need to understand about a man like this, and you'll hear it from me because I'm not going to let you stand there going soft."

She crouched beside the wounded man, not too close, a respectful distance for someone who had been shot through the leg by a stranger with no interest in conversation.

"Thigh wound, clean entry, the shaft is still in him, so the bleeding is actually manageable. That's the bad news for his survival, because it means whoever put that in him didn't care enough to finish it, or didn't have a good enough angle." She traced the line of the wound with her eyes, not her fingers. "The spear has pushed against the femur. He's got a lot of pain and not much time."

She looked at Corvin then, really looked, and her expression did something complicated and fast that would have been unreadable on most faces.

"He's afraid," she said. "That's the second thing. Everyone's afraid. Even the ones who don't show it. This one's showing it, because his hands are doing that thing where they keep trying to grip the grass." She gestured to the wound, to the dirt being disturbed by his fingers. "He doesn't have the strength to do anything about it, but his body still wants to."

Wrack stood again, knees cracking.

"Here's what you need to know for your decision, since you've already made it." She counted on her fingers. "One: he's going to die tonight either way, and if you don't, he'll spend the rest of his dying hour doing it in front of you. Two: if you do it now, properly, it takes less time than you think and less noise than you hope. Three: if you do it badly, you'll spend the next hour apologising to a dead man, and I've seen that too, and it's worse."

She shifted her weight.

"Short spear. Behind him. Above the knee. Push until it stops being pushable. Then pull out the long one from his thigh while you're there, because leaving it in means dragging it along the ground when you walk away, and noise is the one thing we can't afford."

She waited, standing there in the dying light, mud-caked and patient in the way of people who had given up on being anything else.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow and pick up the short spear. My hands are steady. That surprises me. "Above the knee," I repeat, more to myself than to her. Then I move around behind him.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved to stand where she could see him without forcing him to turn and look at her. It was a small accommodation, but it was hers to give and she gave it.

"Feel for the soft spot," she said, keeping her voice level. "Not for the bone. The bone will tell you you're close, but you want the tissue before it, between the joint and the thigh. You'll know it because your hand will sink in slightly."

She watched his hands, the way she watched everything. They were steady. That was either good training or good fear, and in the field the two looked identical.

"Think about something else while you do it," she added, because she remembered being young enough to not know that yet. "Not the push itself. You can't un-think the push. Think about the horses coming home, the grain being loaded, tomorrow's road. Something with a shape to it. Something that finishes."

The light was going fast now, the sky over the tree line turning the colour of old copper. Somewhere behind them, the grey mare shifted her weight and made a soft whinnying sound, and Wrack made a note to check the hitching knot later.

"He's still trying to grip the grass," she said, because that was what she had to say while he did what he had to do. "You can tell him it's done when you're ready. Some men like to hear that. He won't be able to answer, but the saying of it goes somewhere that matters."

She stood with her arms crossed, waiting, her face arranged into nothing in particular.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack uncrossed her arms. She studied him for a long moment, then nodded once, slowly.

"Right," she said. "Straight it is."

She knelt beside the man's legs, keeping her distance from the spear shaft but close enough to gesture at the anatomy of the thigh.

"Soft tissue first. Skin, then fat, then the muscle layer, that's a lot of muscle up here, the quadriceps, the adductors. You'll feel it give, and it'll give more than you expect. It's like pushing your thumb into a ripe peach." She paused, choosing the analogy with care. "Then you'll hit the femur. That's the stop. That's where the spear shaft goes into bone and doesn't go further, which is exactly what you want, because past the femur is the popliteal artery and a mess of things that will make the ground look like a butcher's floor."

She pointed at the area above his knee joint.

"The knee itself is a hinge. Too many joints, too much complexity. You'll miss or you'll hit something that takes a long time to kill and makes a long, loud death. Above the joint, behind the thigh, that's where you want. Clean push, straight in, no twisting. Twisting makes a wound that bleeds wrong, sideways and ugly, and ugly bleeds out over hours instead of minutes."

She looked up at him then.

"It's not like the stories. There's no fountain. No dramatic spray. It's wet and warm and it soaks into the grass before you've finished pulling the spear out, and then it stops being spectacular and just becomes a mess you have to stand in."

She stood and brushed the dirt from her knees again, the same gesture she always made, as though the act of cleaning herself after describing blood could somehow keep the description from sticking to her.

"You'll hear him breathe differently," she added. "Not a scream, not at first. A change in rhythm. He'll be taking shallow breaths and then one deeper one, and then the shallow ones will stop being shallow. You'll know the moment it's over because the effort in his body will just... stop. Like a lamp going out."

The light had dropped another notch. The field was going grey at the edges.

"That's the straight version," she said. "Now go do it while there's still enough light that I can see you if you need me to."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a breath that feels too big for my chest. Then I position the spear, find the soft spot she described, and push. It gives like she said it would. I don't look away.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched, and she did not look away either.

The spear shaft went in clean, and there was the wet warmth she had described, already soaking the grass in a dark circle around the man's legs. His breathing changed as she had said, the shallow rhythm breaking, one deeper draw of air, then silence where the effort used to be.

She counted to three, then to six, then to ten, before she spoke.

"There," she said. "That's done."

She crouched beside him and reached for the long spear still buried in his thigh, pulling it free with a steady, practiced motion. She set the shaft aside in the grass, then pressed her forearm against the wound for a moment, not long, just long enough to stop the worst of it. The blood darkened against her sleeve.

"He'll be cold in about an hour," she said, standing and wiping her arm on the dead man's cloak from earlier. "The cold doesn't matter. You just need to remember it was done quickly and it was done right, because you'll be thinking about the cold part more than the rest of it, and it's not a thing you did."

She looked at Corvin, who was still standing where he had stood, holding the short spear with both hands as though it had grown heavier.

"You want to put it down somewhere it can't be found by accident," she said. "That's the only other task on the list tonight."

She walked back toward the carts, her boots finding the same squelching mud as before, and began checking the hitching knots on the grey mare again, this time properly, double-tying the loops and testing the tension with her thumb.

"Horses are sound," she called back. "Grain is intact. We leave at first light, or sooner if you want to be gone before the dead ones get company." She paused, tying the last knot with fingers that had done this ten thousand times. "You did it right. That's the straight version of that too."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped and turned back. She looked at the boy kneeling over the man's legs, and something in her face tightened, not pity, exactly, but the recognition of a thing being done badly for the first time.

"Right," she said, and she came back and knelt beside him, close enough that he would have to see her watching rather than imagining she had walked away.

"Tell me," she said, "what you're doing now. What are your hands holding, and where is the blade of it?"

She waited, because he would need to find the words for it himself, and because watching him articulate the act would keep his hands steadier than silence would.

When he described the angle, she nodded. "Too high. You're going for the femur and you'll bounce off and he'll still be breathing, which is the one outcome you can't recover from without doing it again." She adjusted her own position, shifting so that she could see his grip. "Lower. Just below the joint line. Feel for the groove where the shin meets the thigh. That's soft. That's where the blood vessels are, and that's where you want depth."

She did not touch his hands. That was for him to do, entirely.

"He's still making a sound," she said, because it was true and because naming it was better than pretending it wasn't there. "It's a low one. He's trying to speak and he can't. That's normal. It goes on longer than people expect."

The light was nearly gone now. The field had become a flat grey shape with darker shapes inside it.

"Push," she said. "Not like you're stabbing. Like you're driving a nail. Steady pressure, straight down, and when it hits bone you'll feel the resistance change. That's your stop. You do not twist. You do not pull and re-enter. You hold it there while he..."

She let the sentence finish itself in the silence.

"...and that's the part that takes the longest. The spear going in is seconds. The part where his body finishes the work is minutes, and he'll be twitching, and he'll make sounds, and his hands will grip the grass harder than before, and that's all his body doing, not his mind. His mind is already gone. You're killing a mechanism now. Remember that. It's a mechanism."

She watched his face the whole time, reading the thing he couldn't say out loud.

"Sound," she repeated, when he had been quiet too long. "It's wet. Not loud. It's the sound of a boot stepping through mud, but repeated. Each time the body pushes against the wound, there's a soft, sucking noise. It's not dramatic. It's just... physical. Like water draining through a cracked pipe."

The man's hand moved in the grass, fingers curling once, twice.

"See that?" Wrack said. "That's the muscles spasm. It's not him reaching for you. It's not him asking for anything. It's nerves doing what nerves do when the signal stops coming through."

She was very still, very attentive, giving him everything she had in the way of words because she knew, from a decade of this work, that the silence after the act was where most men broke.

"Push again," she said, and her voice was calm as a river. "Hold. Watch."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push again, harder, and the spear slides deeper than I meant it to. The man's breath hitches and gurgles. "How long?" I ask, my voice breaking. "Tell me how long now."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't flinch at the broken voice. She had heard it before, in different fields, under different light, from different men who had all stood exactly where this boy stood.

"Ten seconds," she said. "Maybe fifteen. Hold your breath and count."

She put her hand flat on his shoulder, not to steady him, but so that the contact was there, physical, a tether to someone who was still upright and still thinking about horses and grain and tomorrow's road.

"You're doing the right thing. You're holding it in place. That's what you're supposed to do now."

The gurgling came again, wetter this time, a sound like air being forced through a straw. The man's legs jerked once, a full-body spasm that pulled his torso sideways, and then his hands went slack in the grass, fingers uncurling, releasing.

"That's it," Wrack said. "You saw that? Hands gone. Legs done twitching. The sound's changing."

It was changing. The gurgles were slower now, spaced further apart, each one weaker than the last, like a clock winding down.

"Twenty seconds," she said. "He's not suffering. He's leaking. There's a difference and you need to hold onto it."

The light was gone. The world was shapes and mud and the smell of iron and wet wool. Somewhere behind them the grey mare stamped once and stood still again.

"Forty seconds," Wrack said, because counting aloud was easier than sitting in the silence while a body finished dying. "See his chest? It moves twice more, maybe three. Then it stops being a chest and just being skin over air."

The chest moved. Then moved again. Then lay still.

"Done," she said, and the word was flat and final, a door closing. "That was under a minute. You saw the whole of it. No part left out, as you asked."

She knelt and pulled the spear free with a careful motion, letting it slide out slowly so the wound would close enough around itself to slow the bleeding. She pressed her forearm against the area again, brief, firm, then stood and wiped the dark wetness off her sleeve on the grass.

"You'll feel sick," she said, turning to him. "That's not weakness. That's your body telling you something was wrong, which it wasn't, but your body doesn't know that yet. You'll feel it for a few hours, maybe a day, and then it'll settle into a memory that has weight but no edge."

She looked at his face in the dark, her eyes finding the shape of him by memory of where he had stood an hour ago.

"Walk with me to the carts," she said. "There's water. There's a dry patch of cloth for your knees. And there's the decision of whether we leave now in the dark or wait for the light, and you're old enough now to be part of that decision, because you've done the hard part."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sat down in the mud beside him. Not gracefully. She folded herself into the grass with the joints complaining, and she stayed there, close enough that he could see her, far enough that she wasn't crowding.

"You'll dream about it," she said. "Not the spear. Not the pushing. You'll dream about the sound, mostly. The wet sucking sound, and his hands in the grass, and the way his chest moved twice and then stopped. Those are the pieces your head will pick up and replay when you're asleep and your defenses are down."

She pulled a short stick from the ground and began drawing shapes in the dirt, a habit she had when she needed to keep her hands busy while her mouth did the work.

"Here's the rest. There's a version of this that goes badly, and I need to tell you about that too, because you asked for nothing left out."

She drew a small circle in the mud.

"In three or four years, you'll find yourself in a similar position. Maybe not with a spear, with a knife, maybe with a blade and a man who's not even hurt, just a man who needs to die before your company moves on. And you'll be faster than you were tonight. You'll be sure of it. Your hands will know where the soft spot is before your mind catches up, and that's good, that's the skill part working properly."

She drew another circle, connected to the first.

"But the feeling part doesn't get faster. It stays exactly where it is tonight. The first time it's terror and nausea and the whole world shrinking to the size of his eyes. The second time it's the same, mostly, but you'll have the memory of the first time to hold onto, and that's a different kind of weight. The third time, you'll notice you're thinking about the horses again, the grain, the road, and you'll feel guilty about it, and the guilt will be louder than the actual act."

The stick scratched a third circle.

"That's the progression. It doesn't mean you're getting used to it. It means your brain is doing what brains do, which is find a way to keep working in the presence of a thing that would otherwise stop it cold. You'll start to feel less each time, and some men stop there and think they're becoming something they're not, and some men stop there and start drinking, and some men stop there and go home."

She looked at him.

"I'm not one of those three. I'm somewhere in the middle, and I'm fine with that. But you need to know the shape of what's coming, because you can't fight what you haven't seen."

She set the stick down. The shapes in the mud were already blurring, the edges going soft in the dark.

"Here's what I want you to understand about tonight, properly, because I think you've got the first half and missed the second." She leaned back on her hands. "You didn't kill him. You didn't make a choice about his life. He was dead before you picked up the spear. The spear in his thigh did that. The distance to the nearest doctor did that. The fact that he was a sellsword on a border road in a war that nobody's army wanted to win did that."

She paused, letting that sit.

"You just made it fast and quiet instead of slow and loud. You chose the shape of his last minute. That's it. That's the whole of what you did, and it matters, but it's smaller than the feeling of it, and you'll spend a long time needing to believe it's bigger than it is, because the feeling won't let you believe anything smaller."

The grey mare stamped again, somewhere behind them, and was quiet.

"There's one more thing," Wrack said. "You'll want to tell someone about tonight. Not the details, not the sound, not the hands in the grass. You'll want to say: I did it. I held the spear and I pushed and it was done. You'll say it to the next person who comes along, or to the first drunkard in the next tavern, or to yourself in a mirror, and it will feel like confession and it will feel like proof of something."

She stood up, slowly, and offered him her hand. Her palm was rough and warm and smelled of iron.

"Take it when you're ready. And then we'll go check those horses, and then we'll decide about the dark, and then we'll eat, and none of that will change any of what just happened, but all of it will help, because you're alive and I'm alive and there's grain in those carts and the war goes on whether or not we stop to be horrified by it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at her hand in the dark, then take it. My fingers feel cold. "I'm not hungry," I say, standing. "But I'll help with the horses."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gripped his wrist and hauled him up, her boots finding solid ground through the mud by memory.

"Good," she said. "Not hungry means your stomach's still doing the shaking work for you. Give it until we're moving."

She walked him toward the western edge of the field, where the grey mare stood in a shape of grey on grey, her ears rotating toward them like little satellite dishes. The other horses were nearby, a bay and a dark chestnut, both breathing hard and both keeping their heads low against the wind that had come up with the dark.

Wrack went to the grey mare first. She put her hand on its neck, just behind the ears, and murmured the low sounds again, the ones that had worked before. The mare's nostrils flared, took in the smell of blood and iron and two living people, and then settled.

"Good girl," Wrack said, and meant it, in whatever way she meant things.

She turned to Corvin. "You'll want to check their hooves, the mud's soft, they've been standing since the ambush, and a stone under a hoof means a lame horse by morning, and a lame horse means we walk." She pointed toward the bay. "Start there. You're not touching the grey's front legs, she's the one who decides whether we get away tonight, and she's in a mood."

Corvin went to the bay. Wrack watched him for a moment, then turned her attention to the carts, moving between them with her hands testing the straps, checking the load distribution, listening for the telltale creak of a crate that had shifted during the fight.

The grain was intact. She had checked it before and checked it again now, because checking twice was the difference between arriving with cargo and arriving with cargo and a dead escort and a magistrate's inquiry.

"Anything else on the list?" she asked, not looking up from the third crate.

"The dead ones," Corvin said, from the bay's side, his voice steadier now, the shaking apparently having moved somewhere deeper in him where it couldn't be heard. "You said six. There's still the spear shafts to account for, and the man by the tree."

Wrack nodded. "The spear shafts go in the cart with the other metal, they're worth something to a smith even when broken. The man by the tree gets a hole in the ground, or he gets left, and leaving him is the cheaper option and I've left men before who were still breathing, so don't look at me like that." She straightened from the crate, wiping her hands on her belt. "But tonight he's done, so he just needs a cloth over him and a marker stone, so the next company to pass this way knows there's bodies and can pick the route around."

She looked at the sky. The stars were coming out, thin and early, the war clouds having burned themselves out overhead.

"We leave in two hours," she said. "Dark is fine for the first leg, the road's straight and the next settlement's a day's march. But I want the carts loaded properly, the grain stacked so it doesn't shift, and I want you checking those hooves while I do the rest."

She walked to the nearest cart and began the slow, methodical work of re-securing the loads, her movements automatic, practiced, the work of hands that had done this on a hundred roads in a hundred seasons of a war that had outlived the reasons for itself.

"Welcome to the company," she said, quietly, not aimed at him but aimed at the night in general, as though the night were the new recruit and not the boy with cold fingers and a spear in his future.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel beside the bay, running my hands down its leg. The mud's thick and cold. "I'm checking," I say, more to myself. "I'm checking the hooves." It sounds stupid out loud, but I keep doing it anyway.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard him say it and almost smiled, because it was exactly the right thing to be saying, the small, true, grounding words that a man said to a horse when he was trying to remember that horses were not the thing he had just killed.

"Good," she said from somewhere behind the carts. "The far side of the foreleg, the one closest to the ditch. Mud gets packed under those first, and a packed hoof goes flat fast."

She was working on the bay's harness next, checking the buckles, oiling the worn spots with a rag that had seen better decades. Her movements were unhurried but precise, each one a small ritual of maintenance that kept machines of muscle and cartilage from failing on the road.

"You're doing it right," she called. "Not like a groom, but right. You've got the idea that the animal is a thing with parts that can break, and that's more than half the men I've hired ever had."

The grey mare shifted, and Wrack went back to her.

Corvin kept working. He found a small stone under the bay's right hind hoof, worked it out with his thumbnail, and felt the relief in the horse's leg when the pressure was gone. The bay lifted its foot, set it down again, and seemed to relax a notch.

"Stone," he announced, which was also stupid, but she let it go.

"Good find. Check the left."

She was quiet for a while after that, working through the harness and the straps with the same low concentration she applied to everything, and Corvin understood that this was what Wrack did with silence. She filled it with work. The war had given her a decade of silence to fill, and she had filled it with knives and grain and hoof checks and the mechanical business of keeping people alive long enough for the next thing to happen.

After a few minutes, she spoke again, without turning around.

"The man by the tree. I said cloth and marker stone. I didn't say why, and you're old enough now to want the why."

She set down her rag and stood, wiping her hands.

"Because the next company through here will be another six men with another six spears, and if they find the bodies neatly covered, they'll know it was an ambush and they'll know someone else is already dead and they'll take the wider route. If they find the bodies bare and obvious, they'll think it was a skirmish, maybe a fight gone wrong, and they'll push through, and whatever sent that ambush might still be watching."

She turned and looked at him properly.

"Death is information, kid. It tells the living things about the living. Cover a body and you're sending a message: danger here, turn back. Leave it bare and you're saying: nothing to see, keep going. You'll learn to read that language in the field, and eventually you'll learn to send it on purpose."

The stars were fully out now, and the field was silver-grey and vast and very quiet except for the horses breathing and the grain settling in the carts.

"Finish the hooves," she said. "Then we eat, even if you're not hungry, because you will be hungry in an hour and I'd rather you eat when you can sit still than when you're in the saddle. There's salt pork in the back cart. It's old and it's not much, but it's food, and food is the thing that separates a professional from a victim."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I find the salt pork, hard and greasy in its cloth wrapping. I tear a piece off with my teeth. It tastes like nothing. "What's the message we're sending by leaving now?" I ask, swallowing.
