dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stepped back from the body, giving Del the full sight line the code required. The dead man's eyes were still open, fixed on the flagstone ceiling as though expecting the second challenge to come from above.

"The first exchange passed without blood," she said, her voice carrying the flat cadence of recitation. "He lunged early. His stance favoured the left foot and he committed to a high cut when I feinted the riposte."

She paused, because the pause was also part of the form.

"The second engagement was brief. He recovered his guard and crossed for a thrust at the ribs. I stepped inside the blade's reach and closed with a cut to the throat. The wound opened from the sternum to the left clavicle. He fell before he could draw breath for a word."

Auren turned to face Del directly. "That is the accounting. Eleven now." She wiped the hilt once more with her sleeve, a habitual gesture that had nothing to do with the steel and everything to do with marking the transition. "Do you contest the account, or is it witnessed and done?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my eyes still locked on the wound she described. "No contest. Witnessed and done." I look at her, my voice low. "Eleven. Are you alright?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren regarded him for a long moment, her jaw working slightly as though she were deciding whether the question deserved an answer or a rebuke.

"Being 'alright' is not a term the code recognises," she said. "You ask a duellist whether she is alright, you ask a private question. I am a public function. I am a blade that speaks when it has cut." She sheathed the weapon with a sharp, deliberate sound. "The account is given. The body is attended. That is what I am, in this hour."

She did not soften, but she did not walk away either. That was its own kind of answer.

"Eleven wounds, eleven accounts spoken," she continued, turning back to the dead man to make sure the steward and the physicians were properly arranged around him. "I am told by some that I carry it like a weight. I am told by others that I carry it like a ledger, and I find that a fairer description. A ledger does not weep. It balances."

She met Del's eyes again. "You asked kindly, and I will not pretend not to hear the kindness. But the account is the price of the privilege of the sword, and I paid it before you drew your own blade today. It will be paid again, if there is another day."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's hands stopped their cleaning. She looked at Del with an expression he would probably describe, if he were a man given to descriptions, as something between surprise and the faintest grudging respect.

"The account," she repeated. "You mean to witness it yourself. To stand where I stood and hear what I heard and see what I saw."

She crossed her arms. "The code does not forbid it. It is not among the privileges of a second, but it is not forbidden. A witness may ask to be a witness to the witness." She tilted her head, weighing him. "You understand what you are asking. You will hear eleven accounts in succession, or such of them as I have committed to memory in the words the code demands. You will hear names. You will hear wounds. You will hear the rhythm of a man dying across eleven separate rooms and eleven separate years."

She drew a breath. "I have given the account eleven times. I have never given it to anyone who had not been forced to hear it by obligation."

"Then you will not be forced," she said. "I will give it because you asked and I find that I would rather tell it once more into a willing ear than keep it locked in the cabinet of my own keeping." She straightened her collar. "I will begin with the first, because it is the one I think of least and the one that made me."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, a sharp dip of my chin. "Then let me hear it." I brace myself, hands at my sides. "The first."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Corvane of the Salt Marches," Auren began. "The year of the grey frost, four winters past my twelfth year. He was my master's master, a duellist of some reputation in the northern courts, and he challenged me because I had spoken poorly of his teaching in the presence of his pupils."

She looked at the floor for a moment, then at the ceiling, as though the room were not large enough to hold the distance between then and now.

"His blade was a rapier, longer than mine, and he opened with a disengage I had not yet learned to read. The first cut took me across the shoulder, a clean line from the deltoid to the upper arm. I bled enough to see red running down my sleeve, which is a detail I remember more clearly than I ought."

She resumed her formal cadence, though her fingers were pressed flat against her thigh now, steadying her.

"The second exchange, he pressed the advantage. I parried low, which was the wrong instinct, and his point entered my ribs at the fourth costal cartilage. The wound was shallow, a lance through the intercostal muscle, but it made me gasp, and his thrust followed the gasp into the same line. That was the killing wound. It opened the lung."

Auren stopped.

"I was carried out before it sealed. They kept me alive with poultice and a great deal of noise from the physicians, who believed that if they shouted loudly enough, the blood might not find a way out."

She met Del's eyes. "Eleven accounts. The first one nearly took me, and I have told it perhaps forty times since, and it still sounds like a story I am inventing to frighten a pupil." She paused. "It is the second that I am less sure about. The wound was real. The gasp was real. But I have heard other duellists say the same of their near-misses, and I wonder whether memory sharpens the blade or dulls it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"The fourth costal cartilage, as I said," Auren replied, and there was a flicker of irritation that she allowed herself to show, because precision mattered to her more than comfort did. "Left side. Just beneath the arm's reach when the hand is lowered. I have the scar to prove it, though I will not unbutton my collar in front of witnesses to demonstrate."

She resumed her formal posture, arms folded, chin level. "You ask where it landed, and I have answered. The question suggests you want more than the location. Perhaps the angle. Perhaps the depth."

"The thrust entered at approximately the width of two fingers above the sternum's left edge, at a shallow inclination, roughly thirty degrees from the horizontal. The blade was drawn through rather than driven deep. The physician later said the point had opened the pleura and that I breathed blood for two days before the lung sealed itself against the rib."

She watched Del's face carefully, measuring whether he was absorbing it or simply performing absorption.

"Do you understand what you have asked for now?" she said. "Not the first account, which is almost a fairy tale by comparison. The full ledger. Eleven wounds across eleven years, and I have told you I would give them in order because that is how they are kept. The first was the shoulder and the lung. The second was a cut to the hand of a man who held my master's sword against me during a practice bout gone sour, and he died of tetanus three days later, which was not, technically, the killing wound in the manner the code intends, but it is accounted for nonetheless."

She exhaled through her nose. "You have asked to hear where they landed, Del. You have the right to ask. But I will say plainly, because the code teaches me to say plainly: there is no purpose in this that I can see. No second's duty requires it. No honour is improved by it."

She did not stop, however. She merely set her feet apart slightly, grounding herself, and began again.

"Third account. The man was named Sef, of the river guilds, and he owed my master a debt of honour that had ripened into something uglier over the course of two seasons. He cut me across the palm, then across the forearm, and the killing wound was a thrust to the throat, just below the larynx, which severed the carotid artery." She paused. "That one I remember as pain first and silence second. The silence lasted longer than the pain."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her, my own hands curling into fists at my sides. "I'm not asking for honor. I'm asking because you carry it, and I'm your second." I keep my voice steady. "Tell me about the fourth."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren studied him for a moment, and something in her expression shifted, not softening, exactly, but acknowledging.

"Your second," she repeated. "Yes. You are correct to remind me of that." She uncrossed her arms and let them fall to her sides, an adjustment that made her appear a half-inch shorter. "I was being formal. You have a right to the ledger, as my second, and I should not have framed it as a curiosity you were indulging."

She shifted her weight to one hip. "The fourth."

"The fourth was a woman. Her name was Oresca, and she was not, in the manner the code contemplates, a duellist. She was a physician's wife who had taken up the blade because her husband's practice in the low wards had been threatened by a magistrate's son who believed medicine was a trade for lesser men and his father's favour was the only credential that mattered."

Auren's voice maintained its cadence, but her hands were busy now, working the hem of her sleeve as though it required mending.

"She challenged me because I had defended her husband's reputation in a public letter, and she could not. The code allows no duelling for the defence of reputation, but she had a patron who argued the letter constituted a formal slight, and the slight was accepted before I could object."

"The wound was a cut to the thigh," Auren continued. "High on the femoral artery. She was quick to learn but slow to understand the geometry of a straight sword, and I parried three times against thrusts that would have found my knee had she held her guard properly."

She stopped working the sleeve hem. "The killing wound was a cut across the wrist, the dominant one, which broke the tendon to the thumb. It was not a mortal blow. I want that understood. I severed the tendon and she dropped her blade and screamed, and I stood over her with my point at her collarbone and said the words the code requires, and she wept, and the witnesses looked at me as though I were the one who had been wounded."

Auren looked directly at Del. "I have given that account nine times. Nine times I have said: severed the tendon, not the artery. Nine times I have been asked whether I hesitated, and nine times I have answered that I did not, because the code does not permit a duellist to pause and consider whether the wound is adequate to the occasion. You strike where the steel goes."

She drew a breath. "But I will say to you, as your second, and not as a public function: I have considered it more than nine times."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"The blade severed the extensor pollicis longus tendon of her right hand," Auren said. "It entered at the radial side of the wrist, approximately one breadth of coin below the styloid process, and drew through to the dorsal surface of the third metacarpal. The tendon was cut through both bellies of the extensor. The hand could no longer extend the thumb. The hand could no longer grip a blade properly for a period of perhaps two seasons, after which the tendon, being living tissue, would scar and partially reform, though the full strength would never return."

She paused, because precision required the pause.

"That is what the blade did. It made her thumb useless. It made her grip unreliable. It was not the killing wound, because the killing wound in that engagement was the surrender, spoken aloud, witnessed, and recorded."

Auren looked at Del plainly. "You are right that the code says precisely, not tactfully. But I would note that the code also says the account must be given by the victor, and that I am the victor. I am not the blade. The blade does what it does. I say what it did, in the terms the ledger demands, and I have given you the terms."

She straightened her sleeves, a deliberate gesture of closing. "You asked for the fourth and you have it. The tendon, the wrist, the metacarpal, the seasons of impaired grip. Do you require the fifth, or is your curiosity now satisfied?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I don't need the fifth. I need to know if you've eaten today.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's mouth opened, then closed, then opened again, and for a moment she looked genuinely uncertain how to process the question within any framework she recognised.

"Have I eaten," she repeated, as though testing the words on her tongue. "You are asking whether I have eaten."

She looked around the room, past Del, toward where the steward would be arranging the dead man's body for the physicians. The afternoon light through the windows had thinned to a pale grey, which meant the engagement had run longer than the hour usually allotted.

"No," she said. "I have not eaten."

She said it flatly, as a fact of the day, like the weather or the quality of the steel. But her hand went to her mouth, and she held it there a moment, and Del would have noticed that if he were watching her hands, which he was.

"The code provides for refreshment after the accounting," she continued, her voice returning to its formal register. "There is a table set in the antechamber for the victor and the second. It has been set. It has been waited upon. I have been occupied with the body and the physicians and the witnesses, and then with you, and the food has cooled."

She looked at Del with an expression that might have been the ghost of a smile, or might have been a muscle remembering a shape it had not used in years.

"You are asking me to eat," she said. "Not to speak the account. Not to witness. To eat."

"I have not eaten since the morning," she admitted, because the ledger balanced even its small truths. "There was a cup of tea and a slice of something that was meant to be bread and was, in fact, a disappointment."

She shifted her stance and, for the first time, allowed herself to lean against the wall. It was a small surrender, and she seemed aware of it, because she straightened almost immediately.

"Your concern is noted, second. It is a kindness I was not expecting and did not know how to receive. I will note it in the same manner I note the others: as something that happened, plainly stated, without embellishment." She paused. "And I will go and eat the cold food, because it would be unseemly for your second to be more fed than her principal."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's jaw tightened, but she did not argue. The code was the code, and she had just reminded Del of that principle herself.

"Very well. All of it."

She turned back toward the body, then away from it, choosing the centre of the room as though the floorboards there were a lectern.

"His name was Voss," she began. "He was a man of forty-one years, broad in the shoulder, with a scar along his left temple that he wore with the pride of a man who believed it decorated him rather than disfigured him. He had been a duellist for eleven years and had killed four others before today. He was not, by the accounts I was given, a poor swordsman."

She drew a breath.

"The engagement was arranged for a dispute over a property line that had been contested between his family and mine for three generations. The terms were agreed before noon: single combat, straight swords, three engagements or to the death."

"The first exchange lasted perhaps ten seconds. He opened with a false attack, a feint against my left that I recognised immediately, and I counter-thrust through the opening he left. The point entered at the armpit, the left side, between the third and fourth ribs."

Auren stopped walking. She stood still.

"He did not fall. That is the part I must state plainly, because it is the part that distinguishes this from the others. He staggered, he said a word that I could not hear and will not invent, and then he planted his feet and held his guard. The wound was bleeding, freely, but he was a large man, and the lung had not yet been breached. He had perhaps one minute of fight left in him, and he spent it."

She resumed her recitation, but slower now, each word placed like a stone.

"The second engagement, he came for my wrist. He wanted the hand, because a duellist without a blade is a duellist who cannot continue, and he was buying time. I parried, but his cut took the skin and the tendon on the outside of my right hand. I felt the blade pass through the extensor tendons, and I understood at that moment that I had eleven years of sword-work at risk in a single stroke."

She looked at her right hand, flexing the fingers.

"I did not drop the sword. That is not bravery. That was the code. The code requires you to continue until the engagement is decided or a wound is mortal, and his wound to me was not mortal, it was merely inconvenient."

She paused again.

"He thrust for my throat in the third engagement. I saw it coming. I had time to turn my head, to feel the point against my skin, the cold of the steel on the neck, and then I cut down through the line of his shoulder, which opened the clavicle and reached the subclavian artery."

The words were steady, but her hand was gripping the back of her chair where she had not realised she had seated herself.

"He fell forward. Not to his knees, to his hands, as though he were catching himself from a stumble. The blood came from the shoulder and from the armpit wound and from my hand, and it pooled between us on the flagstones in a shape that the witnesses were not allowed to describe in their reports, because the code forbids such descriptions, and because no one wished to be the one who recorded it."

Auren stood up from the chair abruptly.

"He took perhaps nine seconds from the point of the wound to the cessation of motion. He did not speak. He did not reach for me. He simply went down, and the blood went out, and the room became very quiet in a way that I have only ever experienced four or five times in my life."

She looked at Del. "That is all of it. His name was Voss. The wound was the shoulder, the artery, nine seconds. The account is given."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward, my own hand twitching like it wants to reach for hers. "Nine seconds," I echo. The silence stretches. "And your hand?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked down at her right hand, the one Voss had cut, and turned it over as though examining a tool that had been damaged in use.

"The extensor tendons were severed," she said, in the same flat cadence she used for the ledger. "Two of them, the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor indicis. The blade passed through the radial aspect of the wrist and drew free without resistance, which means the cut was clean, which means the wound was efficient."

She closed her fingers slowly, feeling the slight lag in the index finger's movement.

"It is healed. It healed badly, because the tendons scar differently than skin does, and I have lost perhaps a quarter of my precision in that hand. A blade in the right hand, with this injury, is a blade that telegraphs half a heartbeat later than it should." She met Del's eyes. "I have compensated. I have compensated by being faster with my feet and by choosing engagements where the opening is wide enough that my half-second delay does not decide the outcome."

She flexed the fingers again, deliberately, showing him the small gap in the arc of movement.

"The code does not account for this," she said. "It assumes the duellist's hands are intact instruments. It does not provide for a duellist who has been cut and survived and must continue with a diminished tool. I have argued that point in the tribunal three times. I have lost the argument three times. The code is a blade, and like a blade, it does not care what it is held by."

She let her hand fall to her side.

"Nine seconds," she repeated, picking up Del's words the way one picks up a stone from a streambed and turns it over. "You echo it as though it is a burden. Perhaps it is. I have tried to make it a fact. I have tried to make it arithmetic."

She turned away from him briefly, adjusting the hem of her coat at the back.

"Your hand is steady," she said, not quite turning back. "I notice that. You have been standing in this room for a long time listening to a ledger of wounds, and your hands are steady. That is not nothing."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Confirmed," Del said, and his voice did what it does, which is to carry less weight than it should, fraying at the edges, and Auren heard it plainly.

"Confirmed and witnessed," she repeated for him, because the code required the words to be spoken by both parties and he had given her the first half. "The account of Voss, the property line, the three engagements, the wounds to the armpit and the hand and the shoulder, is witnessed and done."

She stood very still in the centre of the room, and the silence that followed was not the silence of a completed ritual but the silence of a woman deciding what came next, which was not the same thing.

"The second account," she said, then stopped. "You asked for all of it earlier. You asked for the fourth and I gave it, and then you asked for the rest, and I have given you the first and the fourth and the eleventh."

She looked at Del's face, reading him the way she read a blade's edge, searching for the notch, the flaw, the place where the metal had been stressed too thin.

"You are unwell," she said. Not a question. "You have been standing for a long time. You have asked me to give accounts of men and women dying, and you have watched me do it, and your voice is failing at the edges."

She crossed the room to where the steward kept the refreshment tray, the one that had gone cold, and she took a cup of tea and set it in Del's hand with a firm grip on his wrist that was more steadying than it was demanding.

"Drink this," she said. "Then I will continue, or you will tell me that you have heard enough, and I will respect that answer because the code does not require a second to be a martyr to the ledger."

She let go of his wrist and stepped back, returning to her position of formal address, arms folded, chin level, the duellist reconstituting herself from the fragments of the afternoon.

"The second account," she began again, without waiting for the tea to be drunk, because she was not a woman who waited. "The man was named Pael. He was my master's rival in the northern schools, and the quarrel concerned a pupil whom both of them claimed had been properly instructed. He was older than me by some fifteen years and had killed once before, a wound to the chest in a street dispute that the code had technically authorised because a challenge had been spoken, though the words had been shouted rather than formally arranged."

"The engagement was quick. He opened with a thrust at the midsection that I had seen him practice a hundred times in the yard, the feint-and-commit that he used against every opponent who had not yet learned to read his left foot."

Auren's thumb worked against her collarbone, a small unconscious motion.

"The killing wound was a cut to the thigh. High on the femoral artery, the same as Oresca's, I noted, though the geometry was different. His was a draw-cut, sweeping outward and downward, and it opened the artery at the junction with the profunda. He sat down on the flagstones rather than fell, which I remember because it seemed so deliberate, so much like a man choosing a chair rather than losing a battle against gravity."

"He held his blade upright in his hand for perhaps four seconds after the wound. I want that stated. Four seconds of upright blade, and then it slid from his fingers and he said a word, one word, which I will not repeat here because it was not a word the code requires and because it was addressed to me, and I did not wish to be the one who held it in my memory."

She paused, drinking her own cold tea, small sips.

"He lasted perhaps a minute from the wound to the end. He watched the blood pool under his own leg with an expression I can only describe as administrative. He was counting, I think. Counting the seconds, or counting the cost, or counting something else entirely that a dying man does when he has a minute left."

"The account is given. The second is accounted."

She looked at Del's face again. "Drink your tea. You are pale in a way that has nothing to do with the afternoon light."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a sip of the tea. It's cold and bitter, but it's something. "He watched it," I say, the cup trembling slightly in my hand. "And you watched him watch it." I set the cup down. "Give me the third."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren noted the trembling of the cup but did not comment on it, because commenting would have made it worse.

"The third," she said. "The man was named Sef, of the river guilds."

She had begun this account earlier, in a compressed form, but Del had asked for all of it, plainly, without the summaries that she had been giving. So she gave it again, from the beginning, in full.

"Sef was a man of thirty-eight years, thick-necked, with hands like the fists of a man who had spent more time on a boat than in a sword school. He was not a duellist by training. He was a duellist by necessity, because his brother had been killed by one of my master's pupils in a brawl that the code had not authorised and the law had not pursued."

She set her feet apart slightly, the stance she had used for years in practice yards, now deployed unconsciously in this room with its cold tea and grey light.

"The challenge was arranged by his sister, who was more educated than her brother and therefore better able to construct the formal terms. She argued that the killing of her brother constituted an injury to the family's honour, and that the code's provision for 'injury to persons standing in a bond of obligation' applied. The tribunal agreed. I was required to answer."

"The engagement took place on the river steps, in winter, because Sef had insisted on the location, claiming that his brother had died in the river and that the account should be made where the account was owed."

Auren's voice held its evenness, but her eyes moved to the window, where the grey afternoon was thinning further.

"The first exchange: he swung the sword like a man cutting rope. Wide, high, committed. I stepped aside and took the cut on my blade, which was a mistake in retrospect, because the force of his swing drove the steel through my guard and into my palm. The wound was to the right hand, the same hand, the extensor side, and I felt the tendon part under his blade as though it were a thread being pulled."

She looked at her own fingers.

"I have said before that the hand was injured in the Voss engagement. That is correct, but it was not the first time. Sef cut the same tendons seven years before Voss cut them. I healed from the first wound and the scar tissue made the second cut easier, in the physical sense, because the blade followed the old path. The code does not record this. The code records only the wounds of the day."

She resumed the formal cadence.

"The killing wound was a thrust to the throat, just below the larynx. I have said this already. It severed the carotid artery. I will add what I did not say before: it was not a clean thrust. His blade had been in my palm for the first exchange, and his grip had loosened, and the thrust was wild, too high by perhaps the width of a finger, and it entered the neck at an angle that opened the wound wider than necessary."

Auren stopped. She pressed her lips together.

"I remember the sound," she said, and this was not part of the code's required account, but she gave it anyway because Del had asked for what it looked like at the end. "The sound was not the sound of a man dying. It was the sound of a man's blood leaving his body through a hole that was too large to close by any means available to the body. It was a wet, rushing sound, like a tap left running, and it lasted longer than I expected."

"He fell backward onto the river steps. The water was low that winter, and he landed on the stone above the waterline, and the blood ran down the steps into the river, and the river took it, and the river did not care."

She drew a breath that she held for a count of three, then released.

"He said nothing. That is the difference between him and Pael and between him and Voss. Sef said nothing. He looked at me, and then he looked at the river, and then the looking stopped."

"The account is given. The third is accounted." She turned to face Del fully. "You asked for all of it. You have all of it. Three accounts, eleven years of a life compressed into an hour of speech, and your cup of cold tea is still in your hand, and your voice is still fraying at the edges."

She reached out and took the cup from him, setting it on the tray beside hers.

"There are eight more," she said. "If you wish them."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I wipe my mouth with the back of my hand. My knuckles are white. "Yes," I say, the word rough. "The ledger's not balanced until you've spoken them all."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren took the word and held it, weighing it like a coin she was not certain was genuine.

"Then the fourth," she said, "in full, because you have earned the full telling and because I find that the half-accounts I gave earlier were cowardice dressed in formality."

She cleared her throat. The gesture was small but deliberate, a resetting of the instrument.

"Oresca. The physician's wife. I gave you the geometry of the wrist wound before, the extensor pollicis longus, the radial side, the styloid process. I will give you the rest now."

"The engagement was arranged in the back garden of the magistrate's house, because the magistrate's son had argued that the garden was neutral ground and therefore the code's requirement for a formal yard was satisfied." Auren's lips thinned. "It was not neutral. It was the magistrate's garden, and the soil was soft, and it was not a place designed for sword-work, and I said so in my objection, which was overruled."

"She opened with a high cut that had no follow-through. A woman of the low wards who had learned the forms from a pamphlet, not from a master. The cut was committed, full-bodied, and it left her completely open beneath the arc."

Auren's fingers tightened on the table's edge.

"I did not strike her in the opening. That is the part I have not said plainly before, and I will say it now. I raised my blade and I waited, because the code does not forbid patience, and because a cut like hers, a cut with no follow-through, meant she had spent her force and would have to recover. I waited the half-second that a duellist should not wait, because waiting is how a lesser opponent kills you, and I was letting a lesser opponent believe she had the advantage."

"She recovered. She swung again, lower this time, at the ribs, and I parried and stepped inside her guard and drew across her wrist."

The cadence held. But her eyes were closed now, and Del could see the cost of that.

"The tendon severed. I have described it. The hand dropped. She screamed, and I want to be precise: she screamed not in pain but in surprise, because she had not expected to be stopped. She had expected to kill me. The pamphlet had taught her that the first cut was the killing cut, and it had not been, and her whole framework of understanding collapsed in the same instant her thumb collapsed."

"She fell to her knees. Not from the wound. From the grief of being wrong."

Auren opened her eyes. "I stood over her. The code required it. The point at the collarbone, the words spoken aloud, the account given before witnesses. She looked up at me with her ruined hand in her lap, and she asked me, in the broken terms of a woman who had believed in her own cause: why had I not struck when she was open? Why had I let her have her second swing?"

She paused, and the room was very quiet.

"Because I did not wish to kill her," Auren said. "That is the truth, and it is not the code's truth, and I have never spoken it in a formal account, because the code does not recognise that answer. The code recognises efficiency, and patience is not efficient. Patience is a choice made by a person, not a function of the blade."

She pressed her knuckles together.

"I severed the tendon because it was the wound that the code required: a wound that ended the engagement without ending her life. A severed tendon is not a killing wound. A severed tendon is a statement that the matter is concluded, that the blade has spoken, that she will not hold a sword against me again, and that she will live."

"The account is given. The fourth is accounted, and this time it is accounted truly."

She looked at Del. "Five more."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her face, the cost of that truth carved into it. "You waited," I repeat, voice low. "And she lived." I look down at my own hands, still pale and steady. "Tell me about the fifth."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Show me what you mean by shape." Halloway stepped forward, the water sliding off her boots in thin sheets, and tilted the lamp lower. The creature lay on its side, half submerged, its proportions wrong in the way that made your eyes keep sliding off it and finding nothing. Long where it should have been short. Too many joints in the forearm. The head, if it was a head, sat at an angle that suggested the neck had been the last thing to hold.

She knelt and let the light settle on the chest cavity. "That's a ribcage," she said, tapping the bone with a gloved finger. "But it's got eleven pairs. Humans get six. Cows get thirteen. This one's in the middle of arguing with itself about what it is."

She moved the lamp along the flank. The skin there was mottled, not bruised so much as confused, patches of grey and flesh-tone overlapping like a map redrawn in haste.

"Old wound, there. Look." A line of scar tissue ran the length of the torso, and it didn't match the skin on either side of it, like two different animals had been stitched together and the seam had finally given out. "That's not healing. That's something that was put back together after it broke, and it kept breaking after that."

Halloway sat back on her heels and studied the thing's face, which was closed, which was the one mercy the cellar offered.

"Three years I chased this type across the Ashlands," she said. "Never got one this whole. Usually they're half-grown when they surface. This one made it far." She paused, letting the lamp flicker. "Don't touch the head. The jaw hinge on these is worse than anything they put on the back."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I lean closer, squinting.* "Eleven ribs. So it's... trying to be something it's not?" *I glance at the scar.* "Who'd stitch it back together?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the scar again, then at the water, which had settled around the carcass like something keeping vigil.

"Nobody stitches them back together," she said. "They do it themselves. That's the part you're not ready for yet." She pulled a cloth from her coat and wiped the lamp's glass, a habit that meant she was buying time to think. "These things grow in layers. One day you're a thing with six ribs and a reasonable appetite. The next you're got seven, and the next eight, and the growth doesn't stop because it's finished. It stops because the animal dies of the effort."

She gestured at the mottled flank. "Every patch of skin on that body was made at a different time, by a different version of whatever it was. The seam isn't a wound. It's a border. Two growth phases meeting where the old shape ended and the new one started."

Halloway shifted her weight, wincing slightly at the knee. Old injury, old habit of ignoring it.

"Eleven ribs means it was still growing when it died. Maybe still growing when it stopped moving in there." She said it flatly, the way you'd report weather. "Which means the last few hours of its life it was trying to become something else and running out of material to do it with."

She reached out and, with the flat of her blade, pushed the thing's arm further from her. The joint crunched. No blood came. "That's what scares me. Not the shape. The fact it was still changing."

Halloway stood, water sloshing around her boots, and angled the lamp back toward the cellar stairwell. "We've got questions about how it got down here, about whether there's a nest above, about whether anything else is still growing on this property. But first we document, and then we burn it in a place where the wind takes the smoke east, away from the village." She looked at Pike over the lamp's glare. "You've got the kit?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set her jaw and let the lamp swing once, slow, so the light traced the whole of the thing again.

"Six months ago it was," she said. "Before that, maybe not. There's a difference between what it is and what it was, and the answer matters for the paperwork, so I'll give you a straight one." She pointed the blade at the ribcage. "The bone structure underneath, the skull, the hands, those are human. The proportions are wrong, the growth is wrong, but the foundation is human."

She crouched again, finding the thing's wrist. She turned it over, examining the too-long fingers, the knuckles that had swollen into something resembling a second joint.

"Person, yes. Recently, yes. But I'd say it was a person the way a tree is a sapling. You'd recognise the species. You wouldn't recognise the individual."

Halloway straightened and wiped her blade on a rag, careful, deliberate, the gesture of a woman who preferred her tools clean regardless of what had been on them.

"Here's what you need to understand about these." She tapped the floor with her boot, sending a ring of black water outward. "It doesn't start as a monster. It starts as someone who's sick, or hurt, or alone in a way that doesn't show on a face. And something in the ground, or the air, or the bloodline, takes that and starts rewriting it. Slowly. The person still walks, still talks, still comes to the well for water. Nobody notices for weeks."

She looked at Pike steadily.

"By the time the ribs don't match, by the time the skin starts patching itself in new phases, the thing was still a person for a long while before that. So. Yes. That was someone. Recently, it was someone who could still recognise their own mother's voice."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I take a step back, the water cold through my boots.* "If it was someone, shouldn't we... I don't know, say something? Before we burn it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at Pike for a long moment, then let out a breath that wasn't quite a laugh.

"Say something to it," she repeated. "That's the kind of question that tells me you've watched the wrong kind of stories." She didn't say it cruelly. She said it the way you'd note a fault in a fence post.

She crouched again, closer this time, close enough that Pike could smell the cellar water and the sweet, faintly metallic rot beginning to work through the carcass.

"Here's the rule, and it's not mine, it's the rule of every hunter who lived long enough to write it down." She rested her hand on the thing's shoulder, not touching, just hovering above the mottled skin. "When the change is done, there's nothing left to say to. Not because they're cruel. Because the person is gone the same way a river is gone once you dam it. The water's still there. It's just not moving anymore."

She looked down at the closed face. The jaw was still. The too-long fingers were splayed in the water.

"This one died in the middle of becoming something else. That's the worst kind of death for these. It wasn't a monster when it stopped. It wasn't a person when it stopped. It was stuck between, and the effort of that stuck state is what finished it." She pulled her hand back. "There's nothing to say to that. There's a lot to say to whoever put this here, or whoever let it happen, and that's a different conversation."

Halloway stood and holstered the blade.

"Now. If you want to do something with meaning before we burn it, we can look for the person it came from. The name, the family, the trail back to whatever made this happen. That's how we honour the human in it. Not by talking to the thing that replaced them." She picked up her lantern and checked the oil. "You've got the kit, Pike. We document, we burn, and then we walk this property looking for signs of a second case. Because these don't come alone."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp from Pike's hand and steadied it against the wall of the cellar, bracing it with her boot so the light held still.

"Plainly, then." She crouched beside the carcass again, pulling her coat sleeves up to the elbows despite the damp cold. "It was a woman. Probably mid-fifties, based on the bone density in the hands before the growth got to them." She indicated the swollen knuckles with her blade tip. "She lived on this property or very near it. The soil in the water's got traces of ash and old lime, which means someone's been burning things down here for a long time. Maybe she kept livestock. Maybe she burned rubbish. Doesn't matter."

She moved to the feet, examining them where they broke the surface. The toes had elongated, splayed wide, the nails thick and dark, almost hoof-like in the middle two.

"The infection, if you want a word for it, starts in the extremities. Hands, feet. Then it works inward along the limbs. The skin thickens and patches over in stages because the body keeps trying to grow new dermis over the old while the old is still attached." She traced the border between two mottled patches with her fingernail, not quite breaking the surface. "By the time the ribs started rearranging, she'd been changing for maybe a year. A year of still showing her face at the bakery, of still answering when someone called her name, of still being afraid of something she couldn't name because the thing in her was afraid too."

Halloway paused. She was looking at the face now, the closed one, with an expression Pike recognised as something between pity and professional distance.

"Here's what plain looks like." She pulled a small glass vial from her coat pocket, already filled with dark liquid. "I took that from the wound site before I came down here. The substance in there, it's not a pathogen in any sense the old books recognise. It's more like a... instruction. A set of orders the body receives and can't refuse." She held the vial up to the lamp. The liquid was viscous, catching the light like dark oil.

"The body doesn't know how to argue with it. It knows how to obey."

Halloway corked the vial and put it in a padded case on the floor beside her.

"So she grew eleven ribs and no one called it wrong. She grew new skin over old skin and her neighbours thought she'd been sunburned. She grew fingers that didn't close properly and she wrapped her hands in cloth and said it was arthritis." Her voice stayed flat, even, but her eyes stayed fixed on the face. "Then one day the growth reached the chest, and the chest couldn't hold, and she came down here to the dark where she wouldn't have to watch it happen to the rest of her."

She looked up at Pike. "That's what happened. She tried to die in private."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "But she didn't die fast." My voice sounds too small for the cellar. I point to the wall, where there are deep, gouged marks in the stone. "She was down here a while."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed Pike's pointing finger to the wall and studied the gouges.

"No," she said, and the word carried the weight of a correction. "That's not her, doing that. Look at the depth." She held her blade across the marks, measuring. "Those are made with something that had more bone than she had left. Those are the marks of the thing that came after her, not the woman making herself comfortable."

She stepped back from the carcass and moved along the cellar wall, lamp swinging to read each scratch.

"Four marks here. Three there. All at the same height, all facing the same direction, toward the far wall." She paused. "She was cornered. Or something else was, and it was backing into her."

Halloway turned back to Pike, her face hard in the lamplight.

"She came down here to die in private, and that's the part I believed. But she didn't die in private." She gestured at the gouges. "Whatever she became, or whatever was already growing in her, it kept working after she went still. The body kept obeying the instruction even without her mind left to feel it. And something in here, or something that came in here after her, got close enough to make those marks."

She crouched again, this time at the far end of the cellar, where the wall met a dark corner the lamp barely reached. She braced the lantern against the stone and squinted.

"Scratches, there too. And these are different. These are from the inside out. Something dug at the mortar from below." She pressed her palm flat against the wall and felt the damp. "There's a passage. Or there was. Someone, or something, got in through here and got out through here."

Halloway stood and wiped her hands on her coat.

"So the plain story gets a second paragraph. She came down to die. She didn't die alone. And whatever else was in this cellar, it left through a hole in the floor, and that hole might still be open." She looked at Pike, and for the first time her voice carried something other than flatness. It was closer to warning.

"We burn this body, yes. But before we go up, we check the floor. Every plank. Because if there's a second case in this house, it's not above us, Pike. It's below."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once, accepting the request as practical rather than morbid. She moved back to the carcass and began working with her hands, gloved fingers parting the water to expose the flank more fully.

"Start from the top down," she said. "The skin. Under the new patches, the old dermis doesn't disappear. It's compressed. Squeezed flat like a pressed flower in a book." She peeled back an edge of the mottled grey skin with her blade, just enough to show the layered surface beneath. "So the body doesn't shed. It stacks. New growth goes over old growth, and the old growth keeps its texture, its scars, its history, under the new layer like sediment."

She pointed at the forearm. "Feel the depth of it. The forearm alone has four distinct growth phases. You can see the transitions, each one where the skin colour changes and the thickness changes. Four different bodies wearing this arm like a glove."

Halloway moved to the ribcage and used her thumb to press between the extra ribs. They gave, slightly, cartilage still soft.

"The ribs don't just grow longer. They branch. Look at this one." She traced a bone that split into two smaller bones mid-arc, like a finger in a glove that had been sewn wrong. "The growth doesn't know the blueprint anymore. It gets the general order, more structure, more reach, and it improvises. So you get ribs that fork. You get vertebrae with extra facets. You get a spine that curves because the new bones are heavier than the muscles still attached to the old ones."

She moved to the hands, turning the too-long fingers over.

"The joints fuse and unfuse. That's the key thing. The infection doesn't just add bone. It dissolves the joints that should hold and then grows new ones in different positions. So the hand can't close. The fingers can't meet. The knuckles lock at odd angles." She flexed the thing's wrist experimentally, and the fingers snapped to a new position with a sound like dry branches. "This is why the woman wrapped them in cloth. She couldn't grip her teacup. She couldn't hold a door handle. And people assumed it was arthritis because they wanted it to be arthritis."

Halloway stood and wiped her hands again, this time on both knees.

"Under all of that, the organs are intact but displaced. The heart's pushed toward the left hip because the ribcage expanded sideways instead of up. The lungs are compressed, which is why she couldn't breathe properly in the final weeks. That's why she came down to the cellar. The air in there is thinner, lower oxygen, and the growing body wants less oxygen than a normal person does. It doesn't feel like breathing. It feels like rest."

She crouched at the face again, and this time she opened the mouth with two fingers, carefully, examining the interior.

"Teeth. Here's what you need to remember if you meet another one alive." She held the lamp close. The teeth had not multiplied, which surprised Pike, but they had changed. They were longer, the canines extended into points, and the enamel was darker, almost black at the tips. "The teeth don't grow in number. They grow in function. The canines for gripping. The molars flattened for grinding things the jaw can now open wide enough to take." She closed the mouth gently. "The jaw hinge moves. The mandible detaches from the skull and reattaches further back. That's why I told you not to touch the head. If you put a finger near that hinge and it fires, there's no saving you."

Halloway stood, breathing harder than the work warranted, and picked up the vial from the padded case.

"The substance itself, what you'd call the agent, it concentrates in the extremities first because that's where the blood flow is slowest and the body's immune response is weakest. It works inward. Heart last, always last. The mind goes before the heart, but the hands and feet go first." She held the vial up. "So if you ever see someone whose fingers are wrong, whose nails are thick, whose joints click when they walk, you don't wait for the ribs. You act on the fingers."

She set the vial back in its case and secured the clasp.

"That's the detail. That's what's under the skin, what it took, how far it gets. Now you know why I burn these things and why I don't do it quickly."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the lamp back and hold it over the floorboards near the wall. "You think there's a hole here. Right under our feet."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway crouched beside Pike and looked down at the floor through the lantern's glare.

"I think the gouges said there's a hole, and I think the damp on that wall said something's been moving through it recently." She shifted her weight, knee protesting again. "But thinking and knowing are different trades. So we find out."

She reached into her coat and produced a coil of thin wire, waxed, with a small iron weight on the end. She fed the wire through the gaps between floorboards near the far wall, feeling with her fingers for a space where the mortar had been dug away.

"There," she said. She found a seam where the stone had been loosened, a gap maybe two inches wide, running vertically. "This was never a finished cellar wall. This was a partition. Someone built this room and then opened it to something below."

Halloway fed the wire through the gap and let it drop. She counted aloud. "One. Two. Three. Four feet of open space, then the weight hits something." She pulled the wire back up slowly and examined the end. There was a smear of something dark on the iron, not mud, not rust.

"Soft tissue," she said. "Or dried blood. I'll take the sample either way."

She knelt fully now, one boot submerged to the ankle bone, and angled the lamp through the gap. The light caught a stone surface below, wet, slicked, and then nothing. The drop was deeper than the wire suggested, or the wire had hit a shelf.

"Right." She stood and wiped the wire on her coat. "So we've got a passage down here that someone used recently. Which means either the woman came down twice, first to die, second to keep the thing below from getting up, or something else came through that hole and made those marks on the wall when it got out."

Halloway looked at Pike with a flatness that masked the fact she was now very careful about where she placed her boots.

"We document the body first. I know I said that twice. But there's a difference between saying it and doing it while there's a passage under your feet leading to somewhere unknown." She pulled a leather journal from her belt pouch and began sketching the ribcage, the limb joints, the growth phases, with quick, precise lines. "You keep the lamp steady. I'll take measurements. And we do not go below that floor until we've got a plan, and we do not leave this cellar with the body still in it, because if whatever made those gouges comes back for what's left, it's not going to be satisfied with the carcass alone."

She paused in her sketching, looked up.

"You asked for detail so you'd know what to look for. Here's your second lesson. Knowing what the thing looks like isn't the same as knowing where it's going. The woman went down to die. Whatever's below went somewhere else entirely. We burn this body, we seal that hole, and then we find out who lives above ground on this property and who hasn't been seen in a while."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't stop cutting. She worked with short, controlled strokes, opening the chest cavity from the sternum down along the line of the extra ribs, peeling back the layered skin and the branching bone beneath.

"The smell first," she said, because Pike asked for nothing left out. "It doesn't smell like decay yet. It smells like copper and something sweet, like overripe fruit left in a closed room. That's the agent. It's still active in the tissues, still sending the instruction to grow, even now, even with the thing dead." She tilted her head. "That's why the joints still moved when I flexed the wrist. The order to obey is in the flesh, and the flesh doesn't know the mind is gone."

She pushed deeper, separating the displaced organs from the compressed lung tissue.

"Under the ribcage, the muscle has changed. Normal human pectoral, you've got a flat sheet of it, one layer, attached at the sternum and the collarbone." She lifted a flap of the chest wall and held it up to the lamp. "This one has four layers. Each one thicker than the last, each one attached slightly off from where the previous one was. The muscles aren't degenerating. They're being recruited into a new shape. Whatever this body was trying to become had more chest than a human should have, and it was building the muscle for it."

Halloway set the flap aside and reached in with her knife, working carefully around the heart, which sat low and left, pushing against the hip bone.

"The heart itself is normal in shape. That's the mercy. The agent gets the heart last, if it ever gets it. What it does to the heart, I've seen twice in thirty years, and both times it was fast." She didn't elaborate. She didn't need to.

She pulled out a length of tissue from the abdominal wall, pale and thick and veined with a dark network that pulsed faintly, not with blood, with something else.

"Look at this. Under the skin, under the fat, there's a second circulation. Not veins. Something like them, but carrying that dark fluid from the vial. The agent doesn't just sit in the cells. It builds infrastructure. New channels through the body, feeding the growth zones, delivering the instruction to each new patch of tissue as it's laid down." She laid the tissue on the floor beside the carcass. "It's like the body is being rebuilt from the inside while the old one still stands. Two houses in the same lot, and the tenants can't agree on whose rules apply."

Halloway moved to the pelvis, where the lower growth phases had been most aggressive.

"Here's how far it got. The pelvis is fractured in three places. Not broken by trauma, the bone grew through itself. The new structure couldn't fit inside the old, so it split the old apart from the inside, like ice in a pipe." She pointed at the fractures with the tip of her knife. "The legs below this point are the most changed. The femurs have doubled in circumference. The shin bones have secondary growths branching off at angles that have no business being there. The feet, you saw them, the toes splayed, the nails thickened, the arch collapsed. She couldn't walk properly in the last month. Maybe the last two."

She paused and looked at Pike over the lamp's glare.

"Everything under the skin is a construction site. That's the phrase. The body became a building under renovation, and the renovation was never going to finish, because the instruction was always more. More bone, more skin, more reach. It never said stop. It only said go further."

Halloway sealed the incision she'd made, not for the dead woman's sake, but because an open body in a cellar with a passage underneath it was a smell problem and a risk problem.

"You asked for everything. So. Everything. She died with the instruction still running in her tissue, still trying to build the next phase. She was mid-renovation when she went still, and the work continued for a while after her mind left. That's why the gouges on the wall are fresher than the body itself." Halloway wiped her knife on the rag and slid it home. "That's the complete picture, Pike. Now we document, we burn, and we check that hole before the smell from this chest cavity does something we don't want it to do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the journal from her and start sketching the tissue sample, my hand shaking just enough to notice. "It's still building," I say quietly. "Even dead. What if it's not done?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the trembling line of Pike's sketch and said nothing for a moment.

"That's the question," she said finally. "And it's not a question I get to answer from down here, because I've seen it stop before." She crouched again, not to examine anything but to put herself at Pike's eye level. "Here's what I know from thirty years of pulling these things out of the ground."

She gestured at the tissue sample on the floor, the dark network still faintly visible under the lamp.

"The instruction needs fuel. Bone growth, new skin, that second circulation, it all costs the body something. Calories, mostly. Mineral density. The body burns through reserves to obey the order, and eventually the reserves run out faster than the body can replace them." She tapped the vial case. "That's why this one died in the cellar instead of the bedroom. The effort of growing eleven ribs and a fourth layer of pectoral muscle used up what was left. The heart tried to keep the new infrastructure supplied, and it couldn't, and the system collapsed."

She stood and began gathering her tools, the journal back to her, the vial secured, the knife wrapped in cloth.

"But you're asking the right question, and I'll give you the honest answer instead of the clean one." She paused at the cellar stairwell, one hand on the railing. "I've had three cases where the tissue kept working after death. Three. The growth didn't finish because the instruction was strong enough to override the metabolic failure, for a while. Not days. Hours. Maybe a week in one case, and that one was a child, which I will not describe to you in detail tonight."

Halloway's voice stayed level, but her eyes were on the floorboards behind Pike, on the gap she'd found.

"So. It's not done. You're right about that. But it's not done the way a sentence is unfinished. It's done the way a fire is unfinished when you pull the log out of the hearth. There's still heat in the tissue, still charge in the instruction, but it's spending itself down. Fast."

She looked back at the carcass, then at Pike.

"Which is why we don't leave it here overnight. We burn it now, tonight, before whatever's left in those channels has time to do anything with the dark and the cold and the silence down here." She checked her oil again, then her matches. "And we seal that passage before we go. Not because the body's going to crawl out, but because whatever made those gouges knows this cellar, and it will come back, and we don't want it finding an open door."

Halloway started up the stairs, boots sliding slightly on the wet stone.

"Come on, Pike. Document the passage, mark the depth, and then we burn this woman's last shape before it builds any further."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the fourth step and put her hand flat on the stone wall beside her.

"Finish what," she said, not turning around.

"The tissue sample. The second circulation. You said there's still charge in it, still heat. Finish explaining how that works before we burn it." Pike's voice stayed steady, which Halloway noted with the respect she owed a young hunter who could keep her composure while sitting in a cellar where a dead thing was still technically growing.

Halloway turned and sat back down on the step behind Pike, knees cracking, ignoring it. She held the lamp between them so they both had light.

"The second circulation," she said, "isn't a circulatory system in any medical sense. It doesn't pump. It doesn't have a valve mechanism. It's closer to how sap moves in a tree, pressure-driven, passive, responding to gravity and temperature." She pulled the tissue sample from the floor and held it between two fingers, careful. "You see the dark network. In life, it was fed by the agent, the instruction fluid, moving from the original infection site outward through these channels. Think of it as a delivery route. The agent travels the channels, reaches a growth zone, and lays down the next order. Grow here. Thicken there. Branch out."

She pointed at a node in the tissue, a swelling where several channels met.

"Those nodes are where the instruction gets translated. The fluid carries a chemical signature, and the cells at the node read it and respond. New bone. New dermis. New muscle fibre. The node is a translator, not a thinker. It doesn't decide. It receives and executes."

Halloway set the sample down and picked it back up, turning it in the lamplight.

"Here's the part that answers your question. When the body dies, the heart stops pumping blood, but these channels don't need a heart. They need pressure differential and heat. The tissue is warm. It stays warm for a while after death because the metabolic process was so active that the heat lingers." She held up the vial again. "The agent in there, it's not dead either. It's a chemical compound that breaks down slowly. In the right conditions, warm, undisturbed, enclosed, it can keep moving through the channels for hours. Maybe longer."

She looked at the carcass, half-opened now, the layered anatomy exposed under the lamp.

"So the answer to 'is it done', is no. The instruction is still in the tissue. The channels are still warm. The agent is still present and still capable of travelling. What stops it isn't death. What stops it is the body running out of material to obey with. You can't grow a twelfth pair of ribs if the calcium's gone. You can't lay down new skin if the amino acids are spent. The instruction keeps sending the order, and the body keeps failing to comply, and eventually the channels run dry because there's nothing left to move through them."

Halloway set the vial down on her knee.

"But 'eventually' is a long word. And we are not in a position to gamble on it."

She stood and offered Pike a hand up.

"Here's what we do, and I want you to understand each step because you'll be doing this work someday and you'll want to know why, not just what." She began walking back toward the carcass, boots squelching. "One, we gather the tissue samples. Everything with visible channels, everything with the dark network. We bag those separately, sealed, labelled. Because that's the research value. That's the only thing from this body that's worth keeping, and it's worth keeping cold."

She knelt and began cutting strips from the abdominal wall, working methodically.

"Two, we burn the rest. Not just the body. The water too. The floorboards we've disturbed. Anything that's soaked in that copper-sweet smell. Because the agent doesn't just live in tissue. It leaches. It seeps into porous surfaces. Burn the water, burn the boards, and then we seal the gap in the wall with lime and stone, proper work, not a patch job."

She tied a bundle of tissue with cord from her belt and set it in a metal case.

"Three, and this is the part I've never found a clean answer for, we check the passage. Not tonight. Not with that body still half-opened and the channels still warm. We check it tomorrow, in daylight, with two people, with the sealed body three fields away burning in a pit where the wind carries east." She paused, cutting another strip. "If the gouges are fresh, something else is down there. Something that isn't this woman. And I want to find it before it finds us."

Halloway stood, brushed the wet off her coat, and looked at Pike with an expression that was almost gentle.

"Finish it means this, then. The body is a building site. The instruction is still on the site. The foreman is dead but the workers are still warm. We don't leave the site overnight. We burn it down, we take the blueprints, and we walk away before the workers get the chance to finish the job on their own."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the metal case from her, my fingers numb against the cold latch. "Tell me what the workers would build," I say. "If they finished."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set down the strip of tissue she'd been cutting and wiped her hands on her coat, deliberate, slow.

"Finished," she repeated. "Let's say the instruction had everything it needed. All the calcium, all the amino acids, all the time. Let's say the body never died, never starved, never stopped obeying. What would it become?"

She walked back to the carcass and crouched beside the ribcage, tracing the branching ribs with her fingertip.

"Start with the chest. You've got four layers of pectoral muscle, each one thicker, each one attached further out from the sternum. Follow the logic of that. Layer five. Layer six. The chest widens until it's a cage of its own, and inside it the lungs are still compressed, still squeezed flat, because the growth doesn't care about breathing. The instruction says expand structure. It doesn't say maintain function."

She moved to the arm, flexing the too-long forearm again, listening to the joints click.

"The limb growth goes for reach. Eleven ribs means the torso's wider. The arms are already too long for the body's height. Follow that outward. The forearms keep growing. The fingers keep splitting and branching because the joints fuse and unfuse and the new growth doesn't respect the old geometry. You get hands that spread wide, hands that can grip things larger than a human hand should grip. Hands that can hold a whole animal, or a whole person, and don't close tight enough to kill quickly."

Halloway's voice stayed flat, but her eyes tracked the limbs as she described them.

"The legs, you saw the femurs doubled. The shins with their secondary growths. If that continues, the legs grow for weight-bearing, for stability under a body that keeps getting heavier. The feet splay wider. The arches collapse further. Eventually the feet are flat, broad, planted, like hooves that haven't decided to be hooves yet."

She stood and looked at the whole carcass, taking it in from the closed face to the splayed feet.

"Now the face. This is the part I'm less certain about, because the instruction reaches the skull last, and I've only seen one case that far along." She held the lamp higher, angling it at the jaw. "The canines extended. The mandible shifted back. The teeth flattened for grinding. If that continues, the jaw grows wider, the palate deepens. The nose flattens because the facial bones are being pulled outward by the expanding skull. The eyes, the eyes get pushed back into the skull to make room for the brain case, which also grows, because the instruction wants more processing power for the new body."

She lowered the lamp.

"None of it is a person. That's the important part. None of it is a monster in the way the old stories meant. It's a thing that keeps growing because it was told to grow and has nothing else to do. It's a building that never gets a roof because the builder is only ever building walls."

Halloway picked up the last strip of tissue and sealed the case with a click.

"Where would it end? If it had time and material, I'd say it ends when the structure can't support itself. The weight exceeds the bone density. The muscle mass outgrows the blood supply. The thing collapses under its own expansion and the agent, the instruction, finally runs out of warm tissue to travel through." She shouldered the case. "That's the natural death of one of these. Not killed. Not burned. Simply too big to stand."

She looked at Pike, standing on the cellar steps with numb fingers and a steady lamp.

"But you're not asking me that to learn a taxonomy. You're asking because you want to know what you'd be looking at if you met one that was closer to finished. So here's the field sign. You don't look for the shape. You look for the weight. These things get heavy before they get fast. A finished one, a near-finished one, it doesn't charge you. It can't. It can barely lift its own arms. You find them slow, you find them low, you find them in low places, cellars, caves, ditches, where they don't have to stand upright."

Halloway started up the stairs, and this time she went slowly, deliberately, testing each step.

"Burn the body. Seal the wall. Check the passage in daylight. And if you find something below that's still warm and still growing, you don't try to talk to it. You don't try to understand what it's building. You note where it is, you note how far it's gotten, and you bring the fire back with you."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the dark network in the tissue sample under the lamplight. "So we're not killing it," I say. "We're just... putting the tools away."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped at the top of the stairs and turned to look down at Pike, the lamplight catching the edge of her jaw.

"No," she said. "That's not what we're doing."

She came back down one step, close enough that Pike could see the grey in her temples, the small scar along her collarbone from an old knife fight in the Ashlands.

"The agent is a chemical compound," she said. "It breaks down. It doesn't die. But it degrades. It loses its structure over time, the way a dye loses its colour in sunlight. The instruction it carries isn't a living thing. It's an order written in chemistry, and chemistry obeys time."

She gestured at the tissue sample in Pike's hands, the dark network faintly visible in the glass of the case.

"What we're doing tonight is removing the medium. The agent needs warm tissue to travel through. It needs channels. It needs pressure and heat and living cells to translate its order into growth. Burn the body, burn the water, burn the boards, and you're not killing the instruction. You're taking away the paper it was written on."

Halloway put a hand on Pike's shoulder, brief, firm.

"Think of it like this. You've got a letter telling you to build a wall. The letter can't build the wall itself. It needs hands. It needs a builder. We're not burning the letter. We're burning the hands."

She looked back at the cellar, at the half-opened carcass, at the dark water, at the gap in the wall where the passage breathed cold air upward.

"The agent will be gone within a week if it's isolated. Two weeks at most. The dark network in that sample will fade to nothing in the cold, in the sealed metal case, with no warmth feeding it. That's the mercy of it. It's not a spirit. It's not a curse. It's a chemical reaction with a long half-life, and we're just shortening the half-life by removing the fuel."

Halloway started up the stairs again, this time with the journal in one hand and the metal case in the other, leaving Pike to finish the tissue documentation.

"But you're right to say it that way," she added, her voice drifting down from the stairwell. "Because it matters for the next case. If you meet something alive, still warm, still building, you don't burn it whole and call it done. You cut the channels. You sever the nodes. You make the instruction unable to reach the growth zones even if the agent is still present. You're not killing it. You're taking its tools away."

She paused at the top of the stairs, the light from the kitchen above falling over her shoulders.

"And then you finish the job properly. With fire, and lime, and a prayer that the village above never learns what lived under their floor."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I close the case and stand up, my legs stiff from kneeling. "So we burn the hands." My voice is low. "Then we find out whose letter it was."
