dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good. Bite this." She held out a leather strap, worn smooth at the center from other mouths. "You bite it too. It's not a favor to him, it's a favor to your hearing."

The man was forty maybe, farmer's hands, mud caked to the wrist creases where his sleeves had been torn away. Both clavicles gone in a way that meant he had hit something hard, fast, and flat. The skin had already begun the gray-green bruising that told Sedge the repair window was closing.

"Hold," she said.

She worked the first shoulder with the elevator, feeling for the fragment edges, listening for the crunch of cartilage against bone. The man screamed into the strap. Wick held. The shoulder popped back with a sound like a knuckle cracking in a quiet church.

"Left one," Sedge said, already moving. "You'll feel it move. Don't yank."

It was worse. More comminuted, the bone in pieces that had no clean seam to seat against. She worked for what felt like an hour and was probably fifteen minutes, pushing fragments into approximate alignment, packing the gap with waxed cloth, then wrapping in the spiral fashion that held without cutting circulation. The man was quiet now, eyes open, looking at the tent ceiling with the expression of someone watching weather roll in.

"Done," she said. "He gets morphine, then water, then he lies flat for a week or his arms will remind him he was an idiot." She wiped her hands on the apron. "You can stand down."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding, my arms shaking a little as I step back from the table. "Never seen bone go back together like that before." I look at the man, then back at Sedge. "Will he really keep still for a week?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No," Sedge said. "He won't. But he'll be groaning loud enough that the orderlies will keep coming to check on him, and being checked on is a form of lying flat."

She gathered the instruments and dropped them into the basin, the clatter of steel on steel muffled by the water. She ran her thumb along the edge of the elevator to check for nicks. There was one, a small gouge near the tip that she'd been meaning to address since the last campaign.

"Where'd you learn this?" she asked Wick, not looking up from her work. "You held steadier than half the men I've had on the table. No shaking, no flinching when he kicked."

Sedge dried the instruments one by one with a rag that was less rag and more accumulated grime, then slid them into their leather roll. The tent flap stirred and a draft brought in the smell of rain and something burning, probably straw, from somewhere down the field road.

"The bone doesn't care how you feel about it," she said. "It cares that you're there and that you aren't moving. That's the whole skill, most of the time. The rest is knowing where to push."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at the man, who was still staring at the ceiling, breathing in the shallow way that meant the morphine had finally found him.

"Bad like he gets to keep both arms and one lung and most of his dignity, if he plays the part," she said. "The clavicle is forgiving. It's a long bone, it heals on its own schedule, and the schedule is longer than anyone wants." She re-tucked the leather roll under her arm. "The lung underneath took a rib point to it when he went down. That's the part that worries me more than the bone. Pneumothorax in a field tent with no bellows is a coin flip, and this one landed on the side where he's breathing."

She paused, watching the man's chest rise. Slow. Steady.

"Coin flips are for people who don't know the odds," she added, and began walking toward the tent flap, then stopped. "You asked how bad. I'll tell you how bad the tent is. Three more cases coming through before dark. One's a shrapnel gut, one's a femur, and one is a boy maybe sixteen with a bullet in the neck that we're not going to stop because his parents are crying at the triage line and crying is a form of medicine, apparently."

She looked at Wick.

"You still standing, or do you need the bench?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, the taste of leather still on my tongue. "I'm standing." I straighten up, trying to ignore the tremble in my hands. "The boy with the bullet—you're just gonna let him through?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No, we're not letting him through. We're letting him *through*, which is different," Sedge said, pulling the tent flap aside with her elbow so she didn't have to use the hand holding the instrument roll. "Bullet through the neck, yes. But not the carotid, not the spinal cord, not the brainstem. The triage officer did the work of me for once. He marked it with chalk and called it a two-minute job."

She stepped out into the rain, which had started in earnest, drumming on the canvas and the mud and the canvas again.

"Here's what I'll tell you," she continued, walking briskly along the path between tents, her boots finding the hard ground by habit. "You can watch the shrapnel gut and learn what a dead man looks like from the inside, which you should, because knowing is better than not knowing. You can watch the femur and learn how to set a long bone when the patient is conscious and screaming, which is harder than the clavicle case because there's more muscle to fight through. And you can watch the boy and learn that sometimes the worst thing in surgery isn't the cutting, it's the deciding."

She stopped at the triage tent. A young orderly was shouting numbers over the din. Somewhere behind the flaps, a woman's voice was rising and falling in the specific cadence of grief that had been interrupted by exhaustion.

"His parents are here," Sedge said. "They're not in the tent. They're at the line, and they're allowed to stay at the line, because the alternative is they climb over the railing and get into the operating tent and do something stupid, and then I have a body *and* a murder to deal with." She adjusted the roll under her arm. "So we let them cry at the line, we send the boy in, and we pray the chalk mark was right."

She pushed through the triage flap without waiting for Wick, which was rude, but Sedge had stopped being polite years ago, somewhere between the third and fourth winter of this war.

Inside, the shrapnel gut was already on the table, held open by a retractor that had rusted in the middle, its surface pitted. Sedge didn't comment on it. She found a clean apron hanging on a nail, slapped it over her shoulders, and washed her hands in a basin of water that was brown and lukewarm.

"There," she said, pointing to Wick's position beside the table, same as before. "You'll hold the retractor on this one. And Wick, I mean it this time. If you flinch, I'll bench you and you'll spend the night counting the lice in the straw."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good instinct," Sedge said, not turning around. "Imagination is worse than any wound. Imagination has no boundaries."

She peeled the patient's shirt aside with a grip that was firm but not careless, the way you'd handle a bird you intended to keep alive. The shrapnel had come from the front, meaning he'd been facing the guns, meaning he'd been a soldier and not a farmer, though the mud on his boots argued with that. The wound was along the left flank, a ragged crescent roughly the width of a hand, with two more entry points above it, smaller, already cauterized with the field dressing the triage officer had applied.

"Three entry points," Sedge said, reading the wound aloud as she did it. "Shrapnel, cast iron most likely, which means it fragments in ways that are irregular and mean. There's no pattern to the pieces. You can't predict where the next one is." She set down the retractor and picked up the forceps. "The bowel is visible. You see the pale pink? That's the outer wall, the serosa, which is still intact in patches. But where it's dark and swollen, that's where it's torn, and where it's torn, there's fluid in the abdomen. Pus, blood, and intestinal contents, which is a cocktail that will kill him faster than the shrapnel if we don't open it, clean it, and close it."

She looked up at Wick.

"Your hands will be wet before the next sentence ends. That's not a warning. That's a timeline."

She positioned the retractor where she wanted it and pressed Wick's palm flat against its edge.

"Hold. You lift the skin away from the wound, not the wound itself. Think of it like opening a book without tearing the pages. Gentle pressure, steady."

The retractor took the weight of the flank and the flesh peeled back, revealing the work inside. Sedge worked with the forceps, picking out a fragment the size of a lentil from the edge of a bowel tear. She dropped it into the basin. Then another. Then one that was larger, shaped like a crooked tooth, that she had to coax out with a twist of the wrist because it had hooked into the mesentery.

The man was conscious. He had been conscious the whole time, and Sedge had not given him anything because he needed to be aware enough to tell her if the pressure changed, which was a strange thing to ask of a man whose gut was on the table.

"Can you hear me?" she asked the patient.

"Y-yes," the man said, his voice thin and watery.

"Good. I'm going to put my finger in your belly. You're going to feel that. You're not going to like it. You're going to tell me if it hurts more than it should."

She pushed the finger through the opening and felt the warm resistance of abdominal contents, the slick pull of fluid, the wrong texture of a bowel that had been sitting in its own mess for hours.

Wick held the retractor. His jaw was set. He did not shake.

Sedge found the main tear. It ran along the colon, maybe four inches of it, ragged at both ends. She cleaned it with a soaked sponge, working the sponge in firm circular strokes, and the smell of it rose even through the rain-damp air of the tent, a smell she had learned to file away the same way she filed away the sounds of screaming and the color of blood pooling under a body.

"You see how the edge is everted?" she said, more to herself than to Wick, but she let him hear it. "That's where you start the sutures. You sew from the clean end toward the dirty end. Never the other way. If you sew from dirty to clean, you drag contamination through the repair and you've built a wall around a garden of infection."

She threaded the needle and began closing, each stitch deliberate, the thread pulled taut but not strangling. Wick watched the needle pass through tissue and emerge on the other side, and she saw him track it, saw him understanding the rhythm of it, the way a stitch was just another act of holding something together.

"There," she said, tying off the last one. "Colon closed. Now the peritoneum, then the muscle, then the skin. Four layers. Four chances to do it right."

She worked through them with the mechanical efficiency of a woman who had done this perhaps two hundred times now, the count having stopped mattering somewhere around fifty. The skin she closed with interrupted sutures, leaving gaps for drainage, because closed too tight and the wound would seep internally, which was worse than the visible seep.

"Bandage," she said, and an orderly appeared with clean linen.

Sedge wrapped the flank, working the fabric snug but not tight, taping the edges with the cloth tape that left a residue like old glue. The man was quiet now, eyes shut, breathing deeper.

"Four days flat on his back," Sedge said. "Then four days on his side. Then he walks, or he doesn't, and if he doesn't, we send him back to the rear hospital with a note that says 'heal poorly' and leave it to God and the good staff at Saint Anne's."

She peeled the apron off and dropped it into the basin. The water went dark.

"You held well," she told Wick. "Your hand never moved. The retractor stayed level the whole time."

She looked at him then, really looked, the way she did after a case when she was deciding whether to send someone to the mess tent for a drink or send them home.

"The neck boy is next," she said. "And the femur is already being prepped behind us. So unless you've had enough, come on."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I don't look away from the basin. "I've had enough," I say, but I'm already following her. "How do you know when the chalk mark's wrong?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled the flap aside for him, rain sheeting off her shoulders, and let him follow without comment.

"You don't," she said, stepping over a coil of rope and a crate of morphine that was chained to the ground with a padlock, a small mercy in a world that had run out of larger ones. "You find out. Usually after you've opened the neck and found the artery is torn in three places, and then you stand there with a patient whose blood is going to drain out of him in the time it takes you to find a clamp, and you learn that the chalk mark was wrong."

She stopped outside the second operating tent, where two orderlies were arguing over a stretcher. The boy was on it, face pale under the grime, a dark stain spreading across the left side of his neck from collarbone to jaw.

"Mark says clean entry, lateral, no major vessel involvement," Sedge said, reading the chalk from a distance. "I don't trust marks."

She stepped inside and the tent was smaller than the last one, closer to the ground, the canvas sagging in the middle. A lamp hung from a nail and swung slightly with the wind. The boy was awake. He was maybe sixteen, maybe seventeen, all elbows and wrists, with a soldier's uniform that had been on him so long it had become skin.

"Can you tell me your name?" Sedge asked him.

"Ellis," he said. "Thomas Ellis. Second battalion."

"Thomas," Sedge said. "I'm going to put my hand on your neck. I'm going to feel for where the bullet went. It doesn't hurt much, just pressure. You're going to tell me if it hurts."

She laid her fingers on the wound site and worked inward, feeling for the tract, the tissue density, the faint heat of a path where something had passed through. The entry was lateral, as marked, but the exit was lower than she expected, near the clavicle, where the subclavian artery ran under a shelf of bone.

"Okay," she said, and looked at Wick, who had been standing just inside the flap, not far enough away to not see, not close enough to be useful. "He's right here. Come closer. You want to learn what the chalk mark being wrong looks like, this is your chance to see the chalk mark being *almost* right."

She cleaned the area with iodine, the brown sting visible on his skin. She laid out the instruments: scalpel, scissors, the retractors, the forceps, and a pair of hemostats that were slightly too long for the space she anticipated.

"Entry is here," she said, pointing. "Exit is here." She tapped the clavicle. "The bullet went through the neck and out through the lower neck, which means it traveled through muscle and fascia and possibly the carotid sheath, which contains the artery, the vein, and the vagus nerve. The vagus nerve controls swallowing and voice. If I've nicked that, he'll have trouble talking for a while, but he'll live. If I've nicked the carotid, he'll have trouble living, period."

She made the incision along the bullet's path, short and deliberate, and the wound opened like a small book. The muscle beneath was dark red, already beginning to clot around the tract.

"There," she said, and Wick leaned in and saw it: the bullet, a lead sphere the size of a bean, lodged against the bone of the clavicle, surrounded by a sleeve of coagulated blood and shredded fascia. It had passed close to the artery. Close enough that the sheath around the vessel was bruised, darkened, but intact.

"Chalk mark was right," Sedge said. "Mostly. 'Mostly' is the word I want you to remember, because in this tent, 'mostly' is how you survive."

She picked out the bullet with the hemostats, felt it rotate as she lifted it free, and dropped it onto the cloth beside the instruments. It rolled and stopped.

"Now the cleaning," she said. "You hold the retractor. Same as before. This time it's a neck, not a flank, so the angle is different. You want the wound open but you don't want to stretch the skin, because skin in the neck is thin and tears easy."

Wick took the retractor and held. The boy watched her work with wide eyes that tracked every movement, and Sedge let him watch, because the alternative was him panicking about what was being done, and panic in a neck wound was its own kind of injury.

She irrigated the tract with clean water, flushed out the blood and tissue debris, and checked the artery again with her fingertip, feeling for the pulse of it beneath the bruised sheath. It was there. Strong and regular.

"Intact," she said. "Now we close."

Three layers, this time. Fascia, then muscle, then skin. She worked fast because the boy was still breathing in the shallow way of a man who had been afraid for a long time and was now too tired to be afraid, which was its own kind of danger.

"There," she said, tying the last suture. "He gets a dressing, then a collar to keep the neck still, then he lies flat until the bruising around the carotid goes down. If it doesn't go down, he goes to the rear hospital, and the rear hospital has a surgeon who can open the sheath and look inside, which I cannot do here."

She washed her hands and stood, wiping them on her apron.

"See?" she said to Wick. "Chalk mark was right. Mostly. And he keeps his voice and his artery and his life, and his parents can stop crying at the line and start crying about something else, like whether he'll be able to eat soup without choking for a week."

She looked at the boy, who was staring at the ceiling again, same expression as the farmer, same weather-rolling-in emptiness.

"Thomas," she said. "You're doing fine. Don't move your neck. Don't try to stand up. Don't be a hero."

The boy nodded, barely, and closed his eyes.

Sedge rolled her instruments and slung the leather roll over her shoulder. Behind them, through the tent wall, she could hear the femur case being prepped, someone shouting about splints and the sound of a bone being broken further because it had been set wrong the first time.

"One more," she said. "Then we all go to bed, which is a luxury, but it's the kind of luxury we have on nights like this."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped in the doorway and turned to face him, arms crossed, rain dripping off the brim of her cap.

"Shrapnel doesn't do one thing," she said. "It does whatever the iron decides. A cast iron shell bursts and the fragments don't fly in a pattern, they scatter like gravel kicked off a boot. One piece might be a sliver, a fingernail wide, and it'll punch through tissue and exit and you'll find it in a dressing days later, barely a scratch. Another piece might be the size of a walnut and it'll turn a man's ribs into a sieve and stop in his liver, and he'll die slowly over three days while his own fluids seep into his own chest and drown him from the inside."

She pushed through the doorway of the third tent. The femur case was already under the lamp, a soldier with his right leg propped on a splint that someone had fashioned from a rifle stock and canvas. The wound was on the thigh, and it was open, which meant they had already done the dirty work of opening it to get the shrapnel out, which was good, which was also bad because that meant the bone was exposed and the bone was visible.

"Here," she said, kneeling beside the table. "Look."

The femur was broken in the mid-shaft, not a clean break but a comminuted one, three or four fragments, the bone edges raw and pink. One piece had been driven sideways into the muscle of the calf, which explained the swelling.

"Shrapnel hits the thigh," Sedge said, picking up the forceps and pointing at the fracture site. "And here's what happens. The fragment doesn't just break the bone. It takes the bone with it. Every piece of shrapnel that passes through bone carries bone dust with it, microscopic particles, ground into the fragment's path like grit in a mill. So when you pull the shrapnel out, you're not leaving a clean hole. You're leaving a track full of ground bone, and that ground bone will seep out through the skin over the next weeks, and you'll get a fistula, which is a pipe of pus and bone chips leaking out of the leg, and the leg will never heal right because the infection has a permanent home."

She probed the wound gently, letting Wick watch the forceps tip disappear into the tissue and emerge with a smear of gray-brown material.

"That's what I'm feeling for now," she said. "More fragments. Shrapnel lodges in muscle, and muscle holds it, and sometimes you can find it, and sometimes it's in the bone itself, inside the marrow cavity, where you cannot reach it without sawing the bone open and breaking it further, and breaking it further is sometimes the right call and sometimes it's a death sentence."

She found a fragment, pulled it free, dropped it in the basin. Another. A third, smaller, that she had to dig for with the tip of a scalpel.

"Then there's the soft tissue," she continued, working. "The thigh has a lot of it. Quadriceps, hamstrings, the vastus lateralis, all of it. Shrapnel tears through that, and the torn muscle is dead muscle, because the blood supply is severed, and dead muscle in a wound becomes an abscess, becomes gas gangrene if the wrong bacteria are present, which they always are, because this is a field tent and not a hospital, and the bacteria here are the bacteria of mud and horse sweat and unwashed hands."

She cleaned the wound with a sponge soaked in carbolic, the smell sharp and medicinal, and Wick held the retractor while she worked, same position, same steady hand.

"So the question isn't 'will the shrapnel kill him,'" Sedge said, tying off the fascia. "The question is whether the leg heals with the bone, or whether the bone heals wrong and he's a cripple, or whether the infection takes the leg and he loses it, or whether the infection takes him and he loses everything. Four outcomes. Sometimes more. And you can't choose which one. You can only do the work in front of you and hope the bone sets and the muscle holds and the fever stays low."

She closed the skin with interrupted sutures, leaving a drainage gap at the lowest point so the wound could weep out rather than rot in.

"Then you splint it," she said, and the orderlies brought the prepped splint, padded with wool, bound with canvas tape. "You pin it, you elevate it, you give him morphine, and then you pray in your own way, which for me is making sure the next patient is ready and the instruments are clean and the lamp has oil in it, because those are the things I can control, and controlling them is the closest I've got to faith."

She finished the bandage and sat back on her heels, breathing hard, which was unusual for her.

"Four cases tonight," she said. "All of them shrapnel or bullet or both. All of them the same fundamental problem: iron goes in, and we try to take it out, and the body decides what it keeps and what it throws away."

She looked at Wick.

"You asked me not to tidy it up. There. That's the untidied version. The shrapnel doesn't matter anymore now that it's out. What matters is whether his body can rebuild what the iron destroyed, and that's not my decision to make. It's a negotiation between his cells and the bacteria, and I'm just the middleman."

She stood, wiped her hands, and began rolling the instruments.

"Go get some water," she told him. "The real kind, not the basin kind. Then come back and help me pack the dead ones, because that's also work, and it's work that gets done whether anyone wants to do it or not."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wipe my palms on my pants, leaving streaks of dampness. "I'll be back," I say, my voice sounding rough. Outside, the rain's cold on my face. I drink from my canteen, trying to wash the taste of iodine and that other smell out of my mouth. I look at my hands for a minute before I go back in.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was waiting outside the tent, sitting on an overturned crate with her instrument roll across her knees, watching the rain slide down the canvas in long dark rivers.

"Good," she said, not looking up. "You look like a man who drank water and not a man who threw it up first, which is progress."

She stood when he got close enough, stretching her back with a sound like old rope snapping. The rain had let up to a drizzle, and the field road was a river of mud that caught the lamplight in dull orange patches.

"The dead ones," she said. "There's six in the wagon at the east end. They went out after the shelling stopped this afternoon, and the stretcher-bearers were busy, so nobody packed them, so they're in there in their coats and their boots and their whatever else they were wearing, and we have to sort that before the morning comes and the mud dries and the flies get in."

She started walking, her boots finding the packed path by memory. Wick fell in behind her, his hands still trembling slightly, a fact she noticed and did not comment on.

"Here's the order of things," she said. "First, you pull the body free of the litter and lay it on the ground. Flat. Face up if possible, because the face tells you more than anything else. Second, you identify. They're all wearing dog tags, but sometimes the tags are bent or the chain is broken and the tags have fallen out, and then you go by whatever is written on the papers in their pockets, which is lucky because most soldiers carry a card, a letter, a photograph, something. You look for the card first."

They reached the wagon, a low canvas-covered thing with iron wheels that had sunk halfway into the mud. Sedge pulled back the canvas with both hands and the smell hit, not the sharp iodine smell of the operating tents but something heavier, sweeter, the smell of a body that had been warm and was no longer.

"Don't hold your breath," she said. "Breath-holding makes you dizzy, and dizzy men drop bodies."

The first was a young man, barely older than the boy Thomas, with a wound in his chest that had been dressed but had failed. His uniform was soaked through with rain and something darker. Sedge worked the dog tags free from his neck, reading them aloud.

"Private. Aldous. Crenshaw." She wrote nothing, because there was no paper, no pencil, because the quartermaster's supply had been burned two weeks ago and nobody had replaced it. "Crenshaw goes in the list. You'll remember it. If you can't remember it, you'll remember it tomorrow when you're angry about it."

She moved to the next body and began the same process, and Wick stood beside her, watching, and then he knelt beside the third one, a larger man with a broken jaw and a coat that had been buttoned wrong before he died, and he found the tags in the collar.

"Major," Wick said, reading. "Holt. R. Holt."

"Write it down," Sedge said, though he had no paper. "In your head. R. Holt, broken jaw, chest intact, which means he died of the jaw, which means he choked on his own blood. That's a slow way to go, and we should be grateful he wasn't the one choking on his own organs instead."

They worked through the six bodies in the rain, Sedge narrating what she did and why, because the sorting was a medical act, not a grim one. She checked wounds, noted causes, made sure each body was positioned so the rain could run off rather than pool. She tied the dog tags together in pairs with string from her apron so they wouldn't scatter in the morning.

"The list goes to the provost marshal," she said, straightening with her hands on her hips. "He sends it to the families, or to the regimental record office, or to the place where names get put on a wall in a church somewhere, depending on how much bureaucracy survives the shelling of the week."

She looked at Wick, and the rain was in her hair, and she was tired in the specific way of a person who had been on her feet for fourteen hours.

"You did it," she said. "You knelt down and you read a man's name and you held it. That's not nothing. That's the part of this that most men can't do, the part where you treat the body like it still belongs to someone."

She rolled up the canvas over the wagon and knotted it tight.

"Go find a bed," she said. "Straw, probably, and probably lice, but it's a bed, and you'll need it." She started walking back toward the medical tents. "And Wick."

He stopped.

"Don't go in there and watch me do it all again tomorrow hoping it won't be as bad," she said. "Go in and expect it to be worse. Expect it to be different. Expect it to be the same. And when you're standing there holding a retractor and your hands are shaking and your stomach is turning, that's when you hold the retractor anyway, because the patient doesn't know your hands are shaking and the bone doesn't care and the shrapnel is already in the man and has to come out whether you feel brave or not."

She pushed through the tent flap and was gone, her boots splashing on the mud path, the lamp swinging in the wind behind her.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Fine," Sedge said, and her voice stayed level even as her hands moved faster. The man on the table was screaming now, a raw sound that tore through the drizzle, and the new fragment had been pulled from his thigh, leaving a hole that bled sluggishly and thickly. "I'm going to tell you everything. You hold him and don't let go."

She set down the hemostats and picked up the scalpel again, this time to widen the wound edges, because the tissue had begun to clamp down around the tract, the body's instinct to close itself fighting against her need to reach the remaining fragments.

"Here's what I'm doing now," she said. "I'm cutting the wound wider. Not because I want to. Because the muscle is sealing itself around the remaining shrapnel, and if I don't open it, I can't see what's left in there, and what's left in there is iron that is grinding against his femur every time his leg twitches."

She made the incision, long and shallow, and the wound opened further, exposing the raw pink interior, the muscle fibers splayed like the threads of a pulled stocking. Wick held the man's thigh, one hand on the knee, one on the hip, bracing the whole length of the limb.

"Here's what's happening inside right now," Sedge continued, feeling with the forceps. "The femur is in four pieces. The main shaft is held together by the periosteum, the membrane that wraps the bone, which is doing its job, thank God, because without it, the fragments would be drifting in the muscle like stones in a river. But the periosteum is torn where the shrapnel passed through, and that means the fragments are loose enough to shift. Every time this man screams, his muscles contract, and the fragments grind against each other, and that grinding is why the wound looks like it does."

She probed deeper, the forceps disappearing into the thigh.

"Found another one," she said. "Small. About the size of a peppercorn. It's lodged in the vastus medialis, which is the inner thigh muscle, and it's pressed against the femur but not in the bone. That means I can pull it out without sawing anything. That means he keeps his leg. That means the outcome is better than it was fifteen minutes ago."

She extracted the fragment and dropped it into the basin. It made a tiny sound, the sound of lead hitting steel, and she noted it with the same attention she gave to everything else.

"Here's what I'm doing next," she said. "I'm going to flush the wound. Clean water, poured in, poured out, repeated, because the wound is full of bone dust and mud and the bacteria that live in both. I'm going to flush until the water comes out mostly clear, and then I'm going to flush one more time because 'mostly clear' is not the same as clean, and clean is the difference between a leg that heals and a leg that gas-necroses in the night."

She called for the irrigation basin and poured water through the wound in steady streams, her other hand pressing the tissue aside so the water could reach the deepest pockets. The man screamed with each pour, and Wick held him through it, his arms locked, his breathing shallow.

"Here's what's happening to his body right now," Sedge said, pausing to let the water drain. "The femur fragments are being bathed in fluid, and the bone dust is washing out, and the dead muscle tissue is being diluted. The living tissue is being preserved. There is a line between those two things, and it's drawn in minutes, not hours. Right now we're on the right side of that line. If I'm slow, if the lamp goes out, if the rain gets in and the orderlies are late with the water, then the line moves, and the dead tissue wins, and the bacteria colonize it, and in three days he has gas gangrene, and gas gangrene in a field tent is a word I say out loud because the alternative is pretending it doesn't exist."

She flushed again. The water was clearer now, brownish but not opaque.

"Here's what I'm going to do next," she said, picking up the sutures. "I'm going to close the wound in layers. Fascia first, then muscle, then skin. Same as the flank man, same as the boy's neck. But this wound is bigger, and the tissue is more damaged, so the sutures have to be stronger, which means I have to use a thicker needle and more thread, and that means I'm slower, and slowness is the enemy here because every minute the wound stays open, another wave of bacteria arrives."

She threaded the needle and began working through the fascia, her hands steady, her eyes on the tissue.

"Here's what I need you to understand," she said, pulling the thread taut. "I am not fixing his leg. I am managing the damage. The femur will heal if it can, and it probably will, but it will heal crooked, because I cannot set these fragments in perfect alignment in a tent with a swinging lamp and a screaming patient. He will have a limp. He will have a shorter leg by half an inch. He will have pain when it rains, which is a thing that happens to people whose bones have been broken badly, and it is not a curse, it is a negotiation with physics."

She tied off the fascia layer and moved to the muscle.

"Here's what I'm doing to the skin now," she said, interrupted sutures, leaving drainage gaps. "And here's what that means: the wound will leak. For a few days, it will weep fluid, blood and serum, and the bandage will soak through, and he will smell, and the orderlies will be unhappy, but the leaking is good. Leaking means the fluid has somewhere to go. A closed wound that can't leak becomes an abscess, and an abscess in a thigh wound is the kind of problem that ends with a saw and a decision that cannot be undone."

She finished the skin closure and applied the bandage, wrapping it in a figure-eight pattern that held the splint in place without crushing the healing tissue.

"Here's what happens next," she said, tying the tape. "He gets morphine. He gets water. He gets a splint and a pillow under his knee and four weeks of lying flat with his leg elevated, because gravity is the enemy of a healing femur and the only way to beat gravity is to avoid it."

She sat back and looked at the leg, at the bandage, at the man beneath it, whose screaming had finally dropped to a whimper.

"Here's what I won't tell you," she said quietly, "because you asked for everything and I'll give you everything except the part I haven't figured out how to say. The bone dust that I flushed out, some of it will stay. It's already in the marrow, ground into the bone itself. His leg will heal, and it will be strong, but it will never be the same leg, and there are men who carry that for the rest of their lives and never complain about it, and there are men who never stop complaining about it, and both are right, and I have no way to predict which one he'll be."

She peeled off her apron and dropped it in the basin.

"That's all of it," she said. "The shrapnel is out. The wound is closed. The leg is splinted. Now he has to heal, and that part is his, not mine."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go of his leg, my hands cramping from the grip. "Will he?" I ask, looking at the man's face now slack with morphine. "Or is he just another one for the wagon tomorrow?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up the leather roll and checked the hemostats one more time before sliding them in.

"He'll live," she said. "The question is whether he'll walk straight or crooked or not at all, and that's a question that has four answers and I only get to pick one of them, which is the one I can do tonight with these instruments and this lamp." She knotted the roll and slung it over her shoulder. "He's not for the wagon. He's for the recovery tent, and then the rear hospital if the bone sets wrong, and then maybe a cane and a limp and a long life of telling people it was a shell that did it, which is true and also an insult to the actual complexity of what happened in there."

She stepped out into the rain, which had thinned to a mist now, and wiped her face with the back of her hand.

"You're asking the wrong question," she added, walking toward the mess tent. "The right question is what happens in the next six hours while his body decides whether to fight the infection or surrender to it. I can't answer that tonight. I can answer it tomorrow, maybe, by looking at the bandage and checking his temperature and seeing if the wound smells like death or like healing. That's the whole medicine of it. You do your work, you leave, and you come back and see if the work held."

She paused under the eave of the mess tent, where a fire was banked low and the smell of boiled vegetables drifted out, which was the closest thing to comfort that existed on this field.

"Four bodies packed," she said. "Four patients treated. Two more on the list for morning." She looked at Wick. "You've been here since before dark and you've held three screaming men and you read a major's name off a dog tag and you asked me to not tidy things up and you listened when I didn't tidy them. That's a long day for a first day."

She pushed through the tent flap into the warm smell of food and the murmur of men eating.

"Sit down," she said. "Eat something. And don't think about the bone dust in his marrow. Think about soup."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge lowered herself onto the straw beside him, not with the casual ease of someone resting but with the deliberate economy of someone whose joints had started to ache. She set the instrument roll between her feet and folded her arms across her chest.

"The rest," she said. "Fine. But it's not one rest. It's a lot of small rests."

She looked at the tent ceiling, where a water stain had formed the shape of a country that existed only in the rain.

"The rest of this war," she said, "is the femur that sets wrong and the fistula that never closes and the leg that comes off in the third week because the gas gangrene was always going to happen, it just took a little longer than I thought. The rest is the boy Thomas, who swallows his first soup and coughs because the vagus nerve is bruised, and then gets better, or doesn't get better, and either way is a life he has to live."

She turned her head and looked at Wick properly.

"The rest is the morning, when the light comes through the tent flaps and the orderlies are already running because they were told the line is long, and I have to open my eyes and count the beds and see how many are occupied and how many are empty, and the empty ones are the ones that mattered yesterday."

She picked at a splinter in her thumbnail.

"The rest is the men who heal. I want to say that clearly, because nobody tells you that part, and it's the part that keeps me here. The farmer with both clavicles. Thomas with his neck. The man whose leg is crooked but will carry him. They heal. They walk. They go home to their farms and their wives and their whatever, and they are alive because someone held a retractor steady and flushed a wound with water and said 'lie flat for four weeks' and meant it."

Her voice did not change. It was the same flat, practical tone she used for suture counts and morphine doses, but she spoke slower now, as if the words were heavier than the air in the tent.

"The rest is the ones who don't. And I won't name them all tonight because there are more than I can hold in my head, and naming them is a job for the provost marshal and a church wall, not for a tent at midnight." She swallowed. "But I'll tell you one thing about the ones who don't. They don't die because of me. That's not true in the way you'd want it to be, but it's true in the way that matters. They die because the iron went in and the body decided to give up, and I did everything I could with what I had, and it wasn't enough, and the next time I'll try again with whatever I have next time, and it won't be enough again, and that is the shape of this."

She leaned back on her hands.

"The rest is also you. Tomorrow you come back, and I'll make you hold a retractor again, and your hands will shake again, and you'll do it anyway, and the day after that the shaking will be less, and the day after that you'll stop noticing the shaking, and one day you'll be standing over a patient and you won't think about whether your hands are steady because you'll be thinking about the tissue, the angle, the next stitch. That's the rest of it. That's the rest of you."

The fire outside crackled. Somewhere a man was coughing in the recovery tent, a wet, rattling cough that meant his lung was working or wasn't.

"You're sitting on the floor," Sedge said. "There's a cot over there. It has lice but it's level."

She stood up, knees popping, and extended a hand.

"Get up," she said. "The rest is tomorrow, and you need sleep for tomorrow, and I need you for tomorrow, and that's the only future either of us gets."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take her hand and pull myself up. My legs feel like they belong to someone else. "Alright," I say, my voice low. "But tomorrow you tell me the rest of the rest."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge held his hand until he was steady on his feet, then let go without ceremony.

"There is no rest of the rest," she said. "There's just the next thing. Tomorrow it's the two on the list, and the ones who come after them, and the ones after them." She turned toward the mess tent, her boots crunching on the mud path. "You want to talk about the rest of the rest, you talk about it while you hold a retractor, because that's when you'll actually have the capacity to hear it."

She stopped at the mess tent entrance, where the smell of soup was stronger now, someone had fed the fire back up.

"Here's what you do tonight," she said. "You eat. You sleep. You don't read books about wounds. You don't go back to the tent and stare at the empty tables. You let the day happen to you, and tomorrow you come back and you hold the retractor, and that's how you learn the rest of the rest, which is that there is no rest of the rest, only the next patient and the next stitch and the next time you hold steady."

She pushed through the flap and was gone, her boots disappearing into the warm light and the noise of men eating and talking in the low, exhausted voices of people who had been awake too long.

Wick sat on the cot for a while, listening to the rain taper off, and tried not to think about bone dust in marrow.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I don't sleep. I sit on the cot with my head in my hands, smelling the soup on my own clothes. I can still feel the way the leg shook under my grip when she pulled that last fragment out.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came back around midnight, which was odd, because she had been in the mess tent an hour ago and there was no reason to return to the sleeping tent unless she was looking for something.

She stood in the flap's shadow, backlit by the corridor lamp, and held up a small tin box.

"I almost forgot to tell you this," she said. She stepped in and set the box on the cot beside him. "You were holding the retractor during the femur case, and you didn't drop it, and you didn't flinch, and I want you to know that I noticed that. I don't usually notice those things. I notice when men drop things."

She sat on the edge of the cot, close enough that their shoulders were nearly touching, far enough that they weren't.

"The tin box has three things in it," she said. "A clean handkerchief, a spare needle, and a note from the surgeon at Saint Anne's who says he's running short of interns and that if anyone's coming forward for the autumn posting, he wants them to write him before the first frost."

She looked at Wick.

"I'm not recruiting you. I'm telling you that the option exists, because you asked me tonight what the rest of the rest is, and the rest of the rest, if you want it, is a hospital in a city with a ceiling that doesn't leak and a supply cart that arrives on Tuesdays and a doctor who teaches instead of just doing." She opened the tin and set the handkerchief and needle on the blanket between them. "But the note is for someone who wants that. If what you want is to hold a retractor in a field tent until your hands stop shaking, then the note doesn't matter, and I'll put it back in the box and we'll both pretend this conversation happened."

The rain had stopped entirely. The air in the tent was cool and smelled of wet canvas and the faint sweetness of the iodine that never fully washed out of anything here.

"Sleep now," she said. "You have two cases tomorrow and I'm not benching you again, and a man who's held three screaming patients but not slept is a man whose hands will shake, and I don't have time to hold the retractor and yours at the same time."

She stood, gathered the tin box, and left it on the blanket, just out of reach.

"If you want to write to Saint Anne's, the paper's in the quartermaster's tent. He's a mean man but he'll give you a sheet if you ask nicely." She paused at the flap. "And Wick."

He didn't look up from his hands.

"You held steady tonight. That's not nothing. It's everything, actually, but tonight it's enough."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I reach out and take the tin, turning it over in my hands. The metal's cold. "I'll hold the retractor tomorrow," I say, looking up at her. "But I'll take the note, too."
